papers.title: Contextualize-then-Aggregate: Circuits for In-Context Learning in Gemma-2 2B
papers.research_question: What mechanism assembles task information from the individual examples in a few-shot prompt during in-context learning?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies a two-step 'contextualize-then-aggregate' circuit for in-context learning in Gemma-2, where lower layers contextualize individual few-shot examples and higher layers aggregate this information to predict the next token.
papers.conclusion: The paper establishes a two-stage procedure for in-context learning where the model contextualizes representations of individual few-shot examples before aggregating them to prepare the next-token prediction.
papers.key_findings:
The model uses a two-step strategy: contextualization of individual few-shot examples in lower layers, followed by aggregation of task information in higher layers.
The aggregation step alone is insufficient for full performance on some tasks; contextualization is crucial, especially with ambiguous examples.
The identified circuits recover at least 90% of the full model's performance across five ICL tasks.
The information transported differs by edge type: aggregation edges generally move task information, while contextualization edges move information about input/output spaces.
The importance and specific edges of the contextualization subcircuit vary between tasks.
papers.limitation:
Analysis is limited to five tasks and one model family (Gemma-2).
Circuit discovery relies on patching, which requires careful design of counterfactual inputs.
The study does not provide a full interpretation of all individual components in the model.
future_direction: Extend the approach to more tasks and models.
Investigate the role of contextualization in other settings, such as linear regression tasks.
Provide a more fine-grained interpretation of individual components.
papers.abstract: In-Context Learning (ICL) is an intriguing ability of large language models (LLMs). Despite a substantial amount of work on its behavioral aspects and how it emerges in miniature setups, it remains unclear which mechanism assembles task information from the individual examples in a fewshot prompt. We use causal interventions to identify information flow in Gemma-2 2B for five naturalistic ICL tasks. We find that the model infers task information using a two-step strategy we call contextualize-then-aggregate: In the lower layers, the model builds up representations of individual fewshot examples, which are contextualized by preceding examples through connections between fewshot input and output tokens across the sequence. In the higher layers, these representations are aggregated to identify the task and prepare prediction of the next output. The importance of the contextualization step differs between tasks, and it may become more important in the presence of ambiguous examples. Overall, by providing rigorous causal analysis, our results shed light on the mechanisms through which ICL happens in language models.

papers.title: On the Emergence of Induction Heads for In-Context Learning
papers.research_question: What are the precise training dynamics during the emergence of induction heads for in-context learning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper uncovers a simple, interpretable structure of the weight matrices implementing induction heads and proves that training dynamics are constrained to a low-dimensional subspace, with only three parameters accounting for the emergence.
papers.conclusion: This work shows how induction heads emerge in an ICL task and paves the way for a better theoretical understanding of transformer learning dynamics.
papers.key_findings:
The weight matrices of an induction head have a simple structure described by three pseudo-parameters (α3, β2, γ3).
Training dynamics remain constrained to a 19-dimensional subspace, and only three dimensions are necessary for the induction head to emerge.
The emergence time of the induction head is quadratic in the context length (Θ(N^2)).
The three parameters emerge in a specific order: γ first, then β, then α.
The emergence of the induction head is self-contained, unaided by the other parameters.
papers.limitation:
Architectural scope is limited to a disentangled, attention-only transformer; production models with LayerNorm, MLPs, and additive residual streams may have different dynamics.
Theoretical results assume orthonormal inputs and zero initialization, which may not hold in practice and could alter emergence times.
The study uses a simplified ICL task (exact matching of item-label pairs), not natural language with its complexities.
future_direction: Exploring how data distributional properties like burstiness modulate the effective context length and emergence.
Investigating other means of reducing effective context length, such as special positional embeddings.
Applying a similar approach to study other phenomena like the in-context vs. in-weights learning trade-off, abrupt learning, or other transformer circuits.
papers.abstract: Transformers have become the dominant architecture for natural language processing. Part of their success is owed to a remarkable capability known as in-context learning (ICL): they can acquire and apply novel associations solely from their input context, without any updates to their weights. In this work, we study the emergence of induction heads, a previously identified mechanism in two-layer transformers that is particularly important for in-context learning. We uncover a relatively simple and interpretable structure of the weight matrices implementing the induction head. We theoretically explain the origin of this structure using a minimal ICL task formulation and a modified transformer architecture. We give a formal proof that the training dynamics remain constrained to a 19-dimensional subspace of the parameter space. Empirically, we validate this constraint while observing that only 3 dimensions account for the emergence of an induction head. By further studying the training dynamics inside this 3-dimensional subspace, we find that the time until the emergence of an induction head follows a tight asymptotic bound that is quadratic in the input context length.

papers.title: Schema-learning and rebinding as mechanisms of in-context learning and emergence
papers.research_question: How does in-context learning work, and can it be explained through schema-learning and rebinding mechanisms in interpretable models like clone-structured causal graphs (CSCGs)?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that in-context learning can be achieved through schema-learning and rebinding mechanisms in interpretable clone-structured causal graphs, providing insights into how ICL works in large language models.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that schema-learning and rebinding mechanisms in CSCGs can explain in-context learning, offering insights for designing interpretable architectures and understanding emergence in large language models.
papers.key_findings:
CSCG achieves in-context learning on the GINC dataset, accurately retrieving latent concepts.
CSCG learns template circuits for algorithms and generalizes to novel tokens through rebinding on the LIALT dataset.
ICL performance improves with model overparameterization, suggesting emergence is related to capacity.
CSCG can inductively learn new word usage from single examples in the dax test.
The mechanisms of schema-learning and rebinding in CSCGs provide a plausible explanation for ICL in transformers.
papers.limitation:
CSCG fails to generalize to concepts unseen during training, similar to transformers.
Imperfections in learned CSCG models can lead to failure cases, such as wrong schema retrieval.
future_direction: Designing novel architectures based on schema-learning and rebinding principles.
Searching for interpretable and editable circuits in transformers using the identified mechanisms.
Extending the approach to more complex tasks and datasets.
papers.abstract: In-context learning (ICL) is one of the most powerful and most unexpected capabilities to emerge in recent transformer-based large language models (LLMs). Yet the mechanisms that underlie it are poorly understood. In this paper, we demonstrate that comparable ICL capabilities can be acquired by an alternative sequence prediction learning method using clone-structured causal graphs (CSCGs). Moreover, a key property of CSCGs is that, unlike transformer-based LLMs, they are {\em interpretable}, which considerably simplifies the task of explaining how ICL works. Specifically, we show that it uses a combination of (a) learning template (schema) circuits for pattern completion, (b) retrieving relevant templates in a context-sensitive manner, and (c) rebinding of novel tokens to appropriate slots in the templates. We go on to marshall evidence for the hypothesis that similar mechanisms underlie ICL in LLMs. For example, we find that, with CSCGs as with LLMs, different capabilities emerge at different levels of overparameterization, suggesting that overparameterization helps in learning more complex template (schema) circuits. By showing how ICL can be achieved with small models and datasets, we open up a path to novel architectures, and take a vital step towards a more general understanding of the mechanics behind this important capability.

papers.title: Mechanistic Fine-tuning for In-context Learning
papers.research_question: How can we efficiently fine-tune language models for in-context learning by directly controlling the attention scores of induction heads, instead of using end-to-end fine-tuning with massive data?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Attention Behavior Fine-Tuning (ABFT), an efficient fine-tuning method for in-context learning that directly optimizes attention scores of induction heads, and shows that this objective is implicit in end-to-end fine-tuning, suggesting a path toward mechanistic controllability.
papers.conclusion: ABFT effectively improves ICL performance by targeting induction heads, and the work demonstrates the potential of controlling model behavior through mechanistic interpretability, opening up the future application of mechanistic controllability.
papers.key_findings:
ABFT significantly improves ICL performance with high efficiency, using only around 0.01% of the data compared to previous methods.
ABFT improves prediction consistency against prompt template and demonstration sampling variations, and reduces bias towards seen labels in unseen-label scenarios.
ABFT is more efficient in time and memory and causes less harm to out-of-domain performance compared to end-to-end fine-tuning.
The ABFT objective is implicitly contained in the end-to-end training objective on ICL-style data, suggesting that such data naturally evokes induction heads.
ABFT demonstrates the possibility of controlling model behavior through intermediate features (attention scores) without supervising the final output, a step toward mechanistic controllability.
papers.limitation:
The induction head-based explanation and ABFT apply only to classification tasks with a finite label set; extending to open-ended tasks remains an open challenge.
The control methods based on gradients and moderate amounts of data are still coarse; future work could focus on gradient-free and data-free model editing.
future_direction: Extending the method to open-ended tasks.
Developing gradient-free and data-free model editing for better mechanistic controllability.
Further improving efficiency by restricting gradient updates to specific transformer layers and automatically optimizing hyperparameters and the induction head filter.
papers.abstract: In-context Learning (ICL) utilizes structured demonstration-query inputs to induce few-shot learning on Language Models (LMs), which are not originally pre-trained on ICL-style data. To bridge the gap between ICL and pre-training, some approaches fine-tune LMs on large ICL-style datasets by an end-to-end paradigm with massive computational costs. To reduce such costs, in this paper, we propose Attention Behavior Fine-Tuning (ABFT), utilizing the previous findings on the inner mechanism of ICL, building training objectives on the attention scores instead of the final outputs, to force the attention scores to focus on the correct label tokens presented in the context and mitigate attention scores from the wrong label tokens. Our experiments on 9 modern LMs and 8 datasets empirically find that ABFT outperforms in performance, robustness, unbiasedness, and efficiency, with only around 0.01% data cost compared to the previous methods. Moreover, our subsequent analysis finds that the end-to-end training objective contains the ABFT objective, suggesting the implicit bias of ICL-style data to the emergence of induction heads. Our work demonstrates the possibility of controlling specific module sequences within LMs to improve their behavior, opening up the future application of mechanistic interpretability.

papers.title: Why Larger Language Models Do In-context Learning Differently?
papers.research_question: Why do larger language models do in-context learning differently? Specifically, why are larger models more sensitive to noise in the test context compared to smaller models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that smaller models emphasize important hidden features while larger ones cover more hidden features, making smaller models more robust to noise and larger ones more easily distracted during in-context learning.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that the difference in ICL behavior between large and small models is due to larger models covering more hidden features, including noisy ones, making them less robust to noise.
papers.key_findings:
Smaller models focus on important hidden features, while larger models cover more features including noisy ones.
Smaller models are more robust to label noise and input noise during ICL evaluation.
Larger models are more easily distracted by noise, leading to worse ICL performance in noisy settings.
Theoretical analysis in linear regression and parity classification settings confirms this behavior difference.
Empirical results on Llama models show that larger models are more sensitive to noise in prompts.
papers.limitation:
The analysis does not extend to real Transformers easily due to high non-convex function and complicated design of multiple-layer Transformers.
The work does not study optimization trajectory.
The experimental verification uses simple binary classification real-world datasets, which has a gap for practical user using the LLM scenario.
future_direction: Study optimization trajectory of ICL in transformers.
Extend analysis to real Transformers with multiple layers and non-linearities.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLM) have emerged as a powerful tool for AI, with the key ability of in-context learning (ICL), where they can perform well on unseen tasks based on a brief series of task examples without necessitating any adjustments to the model parameters. One recent interesting mysterious observation is that models of different scales may have different ICL behaviors: larger models tend to be more sensitive to noise in the test context. This work studies this observation theoretically aiming to improve the understanding of LLM and ICL. We analyze two stylized settings: (1) linear regression with one-layer single-head linear transformers and (2) parity classification with two-layer multiple attention heads transformers (non-linear data and non-linear model). In both settings, we give closed-form optimal solutions and find that smaller models emphasize important hidden features while larger ones cover more hidden features; thus, smaller models are more robust to noise while larger ones are more easily distracted, leading to different ICL behaviors. This sheds light on where transformers pay attention to and how that affects ICL. Preliminary experimental results on large base and chat models provide positive support for our analysis.

papers.title: Counting Hypothesis: Potential Mechanism of In-Context Learning
papers.research_question: How do large language models support in-context learning? What is the underlying mechanism?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes the counting hypothesis, which suggests that LLMs support in-context learning by using context-dependent subspaces to encode potential answers and counting the strengths of contexts across examples.
papers.conclusion: The counting hypothesis offers a plausible explanation for ICL, where LLMs use context-dependent subspaces to encode answers and count contextual strengths across examples, supported by component analysis of residual streams.
papers.key_findings:
Residual streams of separator and answer tokens share common components, as shown by dictionary learning and ICA.
The last separator's residual stream aligns with answer token components, especially in deeper layers.
The coding coefficients of the last separator correlate with the minimum distance between answer and separator components.
The ratio R (based on coding coefficients of top components) differs significantly between correct and incorrect predictions, suggesting embedding components are associated with decision-making.
The counting hypothesis is supported by component analysis of residual streams.
papers.limitation:
The ideal case assumptions (e.g., invariance of example order) may not always hold in practice.
The component analysis methods (dictionary learning and ICA) may not be optimal for extracting the subspaces used by LLMs.
future_direction: Explore effective algorithms to investigate LLMs’ subspace associated with decision-making.
papers.abstract: In-Context Learning (ICL) indicates that large language models (LLMs) pretrained on a massive amount of data can learn specific tasks from input prompts' examples. ICL is notable for two reasons. First, it does not need modification of LLMs' internal structure. Second, it enables LLMs to perform a wide range of tasks/functions with a few examples demonstrating a desirable task. ICL opens up new ways to utilize LLMs in more domains, but its underlying mechanisms still remain poorly understood, making error correction and diagnosis extremely challenging. Thus, it is imperative that we better understand the limitations of ICL and how exactly LLMs support ICL. Inspired by ICL properties and LLMs' functional modules, we propose 1the counting hypothesis' of ICL, which suggests that LLMs' encoding strategy may underlie ICL, and provide supporting evidence.

papers.title: In-Context Learning Without Copying
papers.research_question: Are induction heads a necessary building block for learning abstractive in-context learning (ICL) capabilities, or can such capabilities emerge independently?
papers.core_contribution: Abstractive in-context learning capabilities can emerge independently of induction heads, as demonstrated by the HAPAX training regime which suppresses inductive copying but preserves abstractive ICL performance.
papers.conclusion: The developmental link between induction heads and abstractive in-context learning capabilities is weaker than previously hypothesized.
papers.key_findings:
HAPAX training reduces inductive copying by 66% on random repetition tasks.
Abstractive ICL capabilities are preserved under HAPAX, with the model achieving higher accuracy on 13 out of 21 tasks.
Models trained with HAPAX develop fewer and weaker induction heads.
The token-loss difference metric is primarily affected by exact copying and does not correlate well with abstractive ICL capabilities.
Previous token heads can lead to prefix-matching patterns even in randomly initialized attention heads.
papers.abstract: Induction heads are attention heads that perform inductive copying by matching patterns from earlier context and copying their continuations verbatim. As models develop induction heads, they experience a sharp drop in training loss, a phenomenon cited as evidence that induction heads may underlie a wide range of in-context learning (ICL) capabilities. In this work, we investigate whether induction heads are a necessary building block for learning abstractive ICL capabilities (i.e., tasks where the answer is not contained in the input context), or whether such capabilities can emerge independently. We propose Hapax, a training regime that omits the loss contribution of tokens predictable by induction heads. Despite a significant reduction in inductive copying, abstractive ICL capabilities are preserved, with the model achieving higher accuracy than the vanilla model on 13 out of 21 tasks, even though 31.7% of tokens are omitted from the loss. Furthermore, our model achieves lower loss values on token positions that induction heads cannot predict. Mechanistic analysis shows that models trained with Hapax develop fewer and weaker induction heads despite preserving abstractive ICL capabilities. Our findings suggest that the developmental link between induction heads and abstractive ICL capabilities is weaker than previously hypothesized.

papers.title: Why Can GPT Learn In-Context? Language Models Implicitly Perform Gradient Descent as Meta-Optimizers
papers.research_question: What is the working mechanism of in-context learning (ICL) in GPT models? The paper investigates whether ICL can be understood as implicit finetuning, where the attention mechanism performs a form of gradient descent.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that Transformer attention has a dual form of gradient descent, leading to the understanding that in-context learning is a form of implicit finetuning. Inspired by this, the paper designs a momentum-based attention mechanism that improves performance.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that in-context learning can be understood as implicit finetuning via a meta-optimization process, and this understanding can inspire model design, as demonstrated by the momentum-based attention.
papers.key_findings:
Transformer attention has a dual form with gradient descent, which explains in-context learning as implicit finetuning.
Empirical comparisons show that in-context learning behaves similarly to explicit finetuning in terms of predictions, attention outputs, attention weights, and attention to training tokens.
Momentum-based attention, designed by analogy with gradient descent with momentum, improves performance on language modeling and in-context learning tasks.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is limited to Transformer-based models and does not consider other architectures.
The dual form is derived using a relaxed linear attention approximation, and the mechanism of standard attention without approximation may be more complex.
Experiments are limited to models up to 2.7B parameters and only classification tasks, leaving larger models and other task types for future work.
future_direction: Study in-context learning for non-Transformer architectures.
Investigate the mechanism of standard Transformer attention without the linear approximation.
Extend the analysis to larger models and other tasks like open-ended generation.
papers.abstract: Large pretrained language models have shown surprising in-context learning (ICL) ability. With a few demonstration input-label pairs, they can predict the label for an unseen input without parameter updates. Despite the great success in performance, its working mechanism still remains an open question. In this paper, we explain language models as meta-optimizers and understand in-context learning as implicit finetuning. Theoretically, we figure out that Transformer attention has a dual form of gradient descent. On top of it, we understand ICL as follows: GPT first produces meta-gradients according to the demonstration examples, and then these meta-gradients are applied to the original GPT to build an ICL model. We comprehensively compare the behaviors of in-context learning and explicit finetuning on real tasks to provide empirical evidence that supports our understanding. Experimental results show that in-context learning behaves similarly to explicit finetuning from multiple perspectives. Inspired by the dual form between Transformer attention and gradient descent, we design a momentum-based attention by analogy with gradient descent with momentum. The improved performance over vanilla attention further supports our understanding from another perspective, and more importantly, shows the potential to utilize our understanding for future model design. The code is available at \url{https://aka.ms/icl}.

papers.title: Where does In-context Translation Happen in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Where does in-context Machine Translation occur in GPT models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies a 'task recognition' point in transformer layers where in-context translation is encoded, after which attention to the context is no longer necessary, enabling computational savings by masking context after that point.
papers.conclusion: The study shows that in-context translation is localized to specific layers in LLMs, and leveraging this can reduce computation by masking context after the task recognition point.
papers.key_findings:
There exists a 'task recognition' point in the model layers after which attention to the context is no longer necessary for translation.
The task recognition point occurs at different layers for different models (e.g., layer 25 for GPTNeo, 15-20 for BLOOM, 13-15 for LLAMA).
Critical layers for task location correspond to the middle layers, and masking them causes significant performance drops.
Later layers are redundant and can be masked without significant performance loss.
Lightweight fine-tuning with LoRA is most effective in earlier layers, near the task recognition point.
future_direction: Investigating why GPTNeo has such critical layers compared to other models, possibly due to training data or training dynamics.
papers.abstract: Self-supervised large language models have demonstrated the ability to perform Machine Translation (MT) via in-context learning, but little is known about where the model performs the task with respect to prompt instructions and demonstration examples. In this work, we attempt to characterize the region where large language models transition from in-context learners to translation models. Through a series of layer-wise context-masking experiments on \textsc{GPTNeo2.7B}, \textsc{Bloom3B}, \textsc{Llama7b} and \textsc{Llama7b-chat}, we demonstrate evidence of a "task recognition" point where the translation task is encoded into the input representations and attention to context is no longer necessary. We further observe correspondence between the low performance when masking out entire layers, and the task recognition layers. Taking advantage of this redundancy results in 45\% computational savings when prompting with 5 examples, and task recognition achieved at layer 14 / 32. Our layer-wise fine-tuning experiments indicate that the most effective layers for MT fine-tuning are the layers critical to task recognition.

papers.title: In-Context Language Learning: Architectures and Algorithms
papers.research_question: Which model classes can perform in-context language learning (ICLL), what algorithmic solutions do they implement, and how can architectural changes improve ICLL?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces in-context language learning (ICLL) as a model problem for studying ICL, shows Transformers outperform other models by implementing n-gram heads, and demonstrates that adding n-gram heads improves ICLL and natural language modeling.
papers.conclusion: ICLL is a useful model problem for understanding ICL, and n-gram heads are a key mechanism in Transformers for ICLL that can be used to improve other models.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers significantly outperform recurrent and convolutional models on ICLL tasks.
Transformers develop specialized n-gram heads (higher-order induction heads) to compute in-context n-gram statistics.
Probing shows that Transformers better encode n-gram counts in hidden states compared to other models.
Hard-wiring n-gram heads into other models (RNNs, convolutional) improves their ICLL performance.
Adding n-gram heads also improves natural language modeling perplexity.
papers.limitation: Many aspects of ICLL, even with regular languages, remain to be understood (e.g. learning dynamics and out-of-distribution generalization).
future_direction: Extend ICLL to more expressive languages (context-free or context-sensitive)
Extend experiments to larger models trained with more tokens
papers.abstract: Large-scale neural language models exhibit a remarkable capacity for in-context learning (ICL): they can infer novel functions from datasets provided as input. Most of our current understanding of when and how ICL arises comes from LMs trained on extremely simple learning problems like linear regression and associative recall. There remains a significant gap between these model problems and the "real" ICL exhibited by LMs trained on large text corpora, which involves not just retrieval and function approximation but free-form generation of language and other structured outputs. In this paper, we study ICL through the lens of a new family of model problems we term in context language learning (ICLL). In ICLL, LMs are presented with a set of strings from a formal language, and must generate additional strings from the same language. We focus on in-context learning of regular languages generated by random finite automata. We evaluate a diverse set of neural sequence models (including several RNNs, Transformers, and state-space model variants) on regular ICLL tasks, aiming to answer three questions: (1) Which model classes are empirically capable of ICLL? (2) What algorithmic solutions do successful models implement to perform ICLL? (3) What architectural changes can improve ICLL in less performant models? We first show that Transformers significantly outperform neural sequence models with recurrent or convolutional representations on ICLL tasks. Next, we provide evidence that their ability to do so relies on specialized "n-gram heads" (higher-order variants of induction heads) that compute input-conditional next-token distributions. Finally, we show that hard-wiring these heads into neural models improves performance not just on ICLL, but natural language modeling -- improving the perplexity of 340M-parameter models by up to 1.14 points (6.7%) on the SlimPajama dataset.

papers.title: Structural Supervision Improves Few-Shot Learning and Syntactic Generalization in Neural Language Models
papers.research_question: What is the ability of neural language models to make syntactic generalizations from minimal exposure, and how does structural supervision affect learning outcomes and syntactic invariance?
papers.core_contribution: Neural language models can learn syntactic generalizations from few examples, and explicit structural supervision improves both few-shot learning and syntactic invariance across transformations.
papers.conclusion: Neural language models are capable of inducing syntactic features from minimal exposure and show some invariance to syntactic transformations, with structural supervision enhancing these abilities.
papers.key_findings:
Neural models show robust few-shot learning for nominal number and verbal argument structure after minimal exposure.
Structurally supervised models (ActionLSTM and RNNG) outperform the LSTM model in most syntactic generalization tests.
Models demonstrate syntactic invariance by transferring generalizations learned in base contexts to transformed contexts.
There is a singular bias for nouns and a transitive bias for verbs in few-shot learning, with models assuming default categories when evidence is sparse.
Accuracy often improves with increased exposure for some tests, particularly for structurally supervised models.
papers.limitation: The small training data size poses limitations and suggests the need for scaling to larger datasets for better generalization.
future_direction: Scaling the carefully-controlled methods to larger data settings.
papers.abstract: Humans can learn structural properties about a word from minimal experience, and deploy their learned syntactic representations uniformly in different grammatical contexts. We assess the ability of modern neural language models to reproduce this behavior in English and evaluate the effect of structural supervision on learning outcomes. First, we assess few-shot learning capabilities by developing controlled experiments that probe models' syntactic nominal number and verbal argument structure generalizations for tokens seen as few as two times during training. Second, we assess invariance properties of learned representation: the ability of a model to transfer syntactic generalizations from a base context (e.g., a simple declarative active-voice sentence) to a transformed context (e.g., an interrogative sentence). We test four models trained on the same dataset: an n-gram baseline, an LSTM, and two LSTM-variants trained with explicit structural supervision (Dyer et al.,2016; Charniak et al., 2016). We find that in most cases, the neural models are able to induce the proper syntactic generalizations after minimal exposure, often from just two examples during training, and that the two structurally supervised models generalize more accurately than the LSTM model. All neural models are able to leverage information learned in base contexts to drive expectations in transformed contexts, indicating that they have learned some invariance properties of syntax.

papers.title: Mitigating Copy Bias in In-Context Learning through Neuron Pruning
papers.research_question: How can we mitigate the copying bias in in-context learning, where models copy answers from provided examples instead of learning underlying patterns, by identifying and pruning specific neurons?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method to identify and prune neurons responsible for copying bias in in-context learning, which improves performance across various tasks and models without task-specific data or fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: Targeted neuron pruning mitigates copying bias and improves in-context learning performance across diverse tasks and models, offering a practical post-processing step for deployment.
papers.key_findings:
Copying errors are a significant source of errors in few-shot in-context learning, especially in smaller models.
Neurons responsible for copying behavior can be identified using Integrated Gradients on a synthetic vowel-counting task.
Pruning these identified neurons consistently improves in-context learning performance across a wide range of tasks and model architectures.
Pruning enhances the quality of task vectors, indicating improved task recognition and representation.
The method is practical as it uses a single synthetic task for neuron identification and does not require task-specific data.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive few-shot in-context learning (ICL) abilities. Still, we show that they are sometimes prone to a `copying bias', where they copy answers from provided examples instead of learning the underlying patterns. In this work, we propose a novel and simple method to mitigate such copying bias. First, we create a synthetic task and use the Integrated Gradients method to identify neurons that prioritize copying over generalization. We demonstrate that pruning these neurons consistently improves performance across a diverse set of ICL tasks. We also show that our method is applicable across various LLM architectures, including Transformers and State-Space Models, without requiring modifications. In our analysis, we adopt a task-recognition perspective on ICL and examine task vectors (Hendel et al., 2023) induced by the model. We find that pruning enhances the quality of these vectors, suggesting that the pruned neurons previously hindered effective task recognition.

papers.title: Associative memory inspires improvements for in-context learning using a novel attention residual stream architecture
papers.research_question: How can insights from associative memory models be used to improve in-context learning (ICL) in Transformer-based language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a novel residual attention stream architecture, inspired by associative memory, that allows information to flow directly between attention heads, leading to faster and improved in-context learning in Transformers.
papers.conclusion: The residual attention stream architecture, inspired by associative memory models, improves in-context learning in Transformers and shows promising scalability to larger language models.
papers.key_findings:
A one-layer associative memory model (AMICL) can perform in-context learning on a classification task.
Adding a residual stream for attention values (and to a lesser extent, queries) in a two-layer Transformer speeds up the emergence of ICL during training compared to a classic Transformer.
Naively applying the residual value stream architecture to small language models (8M and 1B parameters) trained on Tiny Stories indicates performance improvements scale to larger models and more naturalistic data.
future_direction: Testing the residual attention stream architecture on larger models and more complex tasks.
Exploring the interpretability of the residual stream for understanding model mechanisms.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) demonstrate an impressive ability to utilise information within the context of their input sequences to appropriately respond to data unseen by the LLM during its training procedure. This ability is known as in-context learning (ICL). Humans and non-human animals demonstrate similar abilities, however their neural architectures differ substantially from LLMs. Despite this, a critical component within LLMs, the attention mechanism, resembles modern associative memory models, widely used in and influenced by the computational neuroscience community to model biological memory systems. Using this connection, we introduce an associative memory model capable of performing ICL. We use this as inspiration for a novel residual stream architecture which allows information to directly flow between attention heads. We test this architecture during training within a two-layer Transformer and show its ICL abilities manifest more quickly than without this modification. We then apply our architecture in small language models with 8 million and 1 billion parameters, focusing on attention head values, with results also indicating improved performance at these larger and more naturalistic scales.

papers.title: The Mystery of In-Context Learning: A Comprehensive Survey on Interpretation and Analysis
papers.core_contribution: This paper presents a thorough survey on the interpretation and analysis of in-context learning (ICL) in large language models, organizing existing research into theoretical and empirical perspectives.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes by discussing open questions and challenges, and suggests potential avenues for future research, establishing the basis for further exploration into the interpretation of in-context learning.
papers.limitation: The survey is limited by space and primarily focuses on the ICL ability, excluding other emergent capabilities such as chain-of-thought and instruction following.
future_direction: Interpretation of ICL in Multimodal LLMs
Interpretation of ICL in Non-Transformer Architectures
Interpretation of ICL in Agentic Systems
papers.abstract: Understanding in-context learning (ICL) capability that enables large language models (LLMs) to excel in proficiency through demonstration examples is of utmost importance. This importance stems not only from the better utilization of this capability across various tasks, but also from the proactive identification and mitigation of potential risks, including concerns regarding truthfulness, bias, and toxicity, that may arise alongside the capability. In this paper, we present a thorough survey on the interpretation and analysis of in-context learning. First, we provide a concise introduction to the background and definition of in-context learning. Then, we give an overview of advancements from two perspectives: 1) a theoretical perspective, emphasizing studies on mechanistic interpretability and delving into the mathematical foundations behind ICL; and 2) an empirical perspective, concerning studies that empirically analyze factors associated with ICL. We conclude by highlighting the challenges encountered and suggesting potential avenues for future research. We believe that our work establishes the basis for further exploration into the interpretation of in-context learning. Additionally, we have created a repository containing the resources referenced in our survey.

papers.title: Understanding In-Context Learning from Repetitions
papers.research_question: What is the mechanism underpinning in-context learning in Large Language Models, and how can it be understood through the lens of surface repetitions and token co-occurrence reinforcement?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a novel feature-centric perspective on in-context learning by identifying and analyzing token co-occurrence reinforcement, showing how surface patterns both enable and hinder ICL.
papers.conclusion: Token reinforcement is a key mechanism in in-context learning, acting as a double-edged sword that can be leveraged to maximize ICL effectiveness with informed demonstrations.
papers.key_findings:
Token co-occurrence reinforcement exists: the connection between any two tokens strengthens with their contextual co-occurrences.
Token reinforcement helps constrain the output space and enables models to follow patterns like chain-of-thought prompting.
Token reinforcement can lead to spurious connections and cause ICL failures when demonstrations contain unintended patterns.
The reinforcement effect scales with model size, with larger models showing stronger distant reinforcement.
Token reinforcement arises from the model's optimization of training likelihood, as evidenced by empirical analysis of pretraining data.
papers.abstract: This paper explores the elusive mechanism underpinning in-context learning in Large Language Models (LLMs). Our work provides a novel perspective by examining in-context learning via the lens of surface repetitions. We quantitatively investigate the role of surface features in text generation, and empirically establish the existence of \emph{token co-occurrence reinforcement}, a principle that strengthens the relationship between two tokens based on their contextual co-occurrences. By investigating the dual impacts of these features, our research illuminates the internal workings of in-context learning and expounds on the reasons for its failures. This paper provides an essential contribution to the understanding of in-context learning and its potential limitations, providing a fresh perspective on this exciting capability.

papers.title: From Compression to Expression: A Layerwise Analysis of In-Context Learning
papers.research_question: How do LLMs extract and differentiate task information from shallow to deep layers during in-context learning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers and analyzes the Layerwise Compression-Expression phenomenon in ICL, where early layers compress task information from demonstrations and later layers express it for prediction, with implications for performance and robustness.
papers.conclusion: This work provides a comprehensive analysis of ICL internal dynamics, uncovering the prevalent Layerwise Compression-Expression phenomenon, which deepens understanding of structured representation learning in LLMs and offers practical implications for interpretability, efficiency, and robustness.
papers.key_findings:
The Layerwise Compression-Expression phenomenon is prevalent across diverse model architectures (transformer and state-space) and task domains (symbolic, language, multimodal).
Larger models and more demonstrations lead to more compressed task representations, explaining performance improvements with scale and context length.
Noisy demonstrations result in less compressed representations, but ICL remains robust up to a certain noise ratio due to distinguishable task vectors.
Attention mechanisms contribute to reducing both bias and variance of task representations as the number of demonstrations increases, as shown in a theoretical analysis.
Task-vector contrastive fine-tuning, motivated by the analysis, can further compress task vectors and improve task-vector accuracy.
papers.limitation: The theoretical analysis uses a simplified linear attention model, sharing the same simplifications and limitations as prior work on linear self-attention.
future_direction: Theoretical investigation of the phenomenon in the infinite-sample regime.
papers.abstract: In-context learning (ICL) enables large language models (LLMs) to adapt to new tasks without weight updates by learning from demonstration sequences. While ICL shows strong empirical performance, its internal representational mechanisms are not yet well understood. In this work, we conduct a statistical geometric analysis of ICL representations to investigate how task-specific information is captured across layers. Our analysis reveals an intriguing phenomenon, which we term *Layerwise Compression-Expression*: early layers progressively produce compact and discriminative representations that encode task information from the input demonstrations, while later layers express these representations to incorporate the query and generate the prediction. This phenomenon is observed consistently across diverse tasks and a range of contemporary LLM architectures. We demonstrate that it has important implications for ICL performance -- improving with model size and the number of demonstrations -- and for robustness in the presence of noisy examples. To further understand the effect of the compact task representation, we propose a bias-variance decomposition and provide a theoretical analysis showing how attention mechanisms contribute to reducing both variance and bias, thereby enhancing performance as the number of demonstrations increases. Our findings reveal an intriguing layerwise dynamic in ICL, highlight how structured representations emerge within LLMs, and showcase that analyzing internal representations can facilitate a deeper understanding of model behavior.

papers.title: Unifying Attention Heads and Task Vectors via Hidden State Geometry in In-Context Learning
papers.research_question: How do attention heads and task vectors jointly shape the hidden state geometry in in-context learning, and can they be unified in a single framework?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a unified framework linking attention heads and task vectors through the geometry of hidden states in in-context learning, revealing a two-stage mechanism where separability emerges early and alignment develops later.
papers.conclusion: The proposed framework bridges the gap between attention heads and task vectors, offering a unified account of the underlying mechanisms of in-context learning.
papers.key_findings:
ICL improves classification primarily by enhancing the alignment of query hidden states with label unembedding vectors, not by increasing separability.
ICL proceeds as a two-stage process: early layers increase hidden-state separability, while middle-to-late layers improve alignment.
Previous Token Heads (PTHs) drive the early increase in separability.
Induction Heads (IHs) enhance alignment in later layers by amplifying hidden state components along the unembedding directions.
The two-stage phase transition pattern is robust across different ICL settings, models, and extends to generation tasks.
papers.abstract: The unusual properties of in-context learning (ICL) have prompted investigations into the internal mechanisms of large language models. Prior work typically focuses on either special attention heads or task vectors at specific layers, but lacks a unified framework linking these components to the evolution of hidden states across layers that ultimately produce the model's output. In this paper, we propose such a framework for ICL in classification tasks by analyzing two geometric factors that govern performance: the separability and alignment of query hidden states. A fine-grained analysis of layer-wise dynamics reveals a striking two-stage mechanism: separability emerges in early layers, while alignment develops in later layers. Ablation studies further show that Previous Token Heads drive separability, while Induction Heads and task vectors enhance alignment. Our findings thus bridge the gap between attention heads and task vectors, offering a unified account of ICL's underlying mechanisms.

papers.title: A Mechanism for Sample-Efficient In-Context Learning for Sparse Retrieval Tasks
papers.research_question: How can transformer models perform in-context learning efficiently, and what are the sample complexity guarantees for such mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a mechanism for in-context learning that includes prompt segmentation and hypothesis learning for sparse retrieval tasks, showing that transformers can implement this mechanism and providing sample complexity guarantees.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that transformers can implement in-context learning mechanisms for sparse retrieval tasks, with theoretical sample complexity guarantees and empirical validation.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers can segment prompts using maximum likelihood segmentation with sample complexity logarithmic in the number of delimiters.
Transformers can learn a consistent hypothesis for sparse regression tasks with sample complexity O(s log(m/ϵ)/ϵ).
Empirical validation shows that ICL performance depends on delimiter choice and attention maps correspond to theoretical mechanisms.
papers.limitation: The paper does not study the properties of the pre-training process and data distribution, which are crucial for ICL.
future_direction: Expanding the theoretical model to address pre-training process and data distribution
Improving the estimator to use prior probabilities from the base distribution
papers.abstract: We study the phenomenon of \textit{in-context learning} (ICL) exhibited by large language models, where they can adapt to a new learning task, given a handful of labeled examples, without any explicit parameter optimization. Our goal is to explain how a pre-trained transformer model is able to perform ICL under reasonable assumptions on the pre-training process and the downstream tasks. We posit a mechanism whereby a transformer can achieve the following: (a) receive an i.i.d. sequence of examples which have been converted into a prompt using potentially-ambiguous delimiters, (b) correctly segment the prompt into examples and labels, (c) infer from the data a \textit{sparse linear regressor} hypothesis, and finally (d) apply this hypothesis on the given test example and return a predicted label. We establish that this entire procedure is implementable using the transformer mechanism, and we give sample complexity guarantees for this learning framework. Our empirical findings validate the challenge of segmentation, and we show a correspondence between our posited mechanisms and observed attention maps for step (c).

papers.title: The Dual-Route Model of Induction
papers.research_question: Do language models have two separate induction routes for verbatim token copying and semantic concept copying, and what are the properties of these routes?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers concept-level induction heads in LLMs that copy entire lexical units, revealing a dual-route induction mechanism where token heads handle verbatim copying and concept heads handle semantic tasks like translation, and shows that concept heads output language-agnostic word representations.
papers.conclusion: LLMs employ a dual-route model of induction analogous to human reading, with separate token and concept induction heads that enable both verbatim and semantic copying, and concept heads represent abstract word meanings independent of language.
papers.key_findings:
Concept induction heads attend to the ends of multi-token words and copy entire concepts, while token induction heads attend to the next token for verbatim copying.
Ablation of token induction heads causes models to paraphrase instead of copying verbatim.
Concept induction heads are vital for semantic tasks like translation, synonyms, and antonyms.
Concept induction heads output language-agnostic word representations, as shown by patching experiments.
The two routes operate independently, with little overlap between top token and concept copier heads.
papers.limitation: The findings on language-agnostic representations may not hold for low-resource languages, as the models were not evaluated on them.
future_direction: Investigate whether concept induction heads emerge in other architectures, such as encoder-decoder models or non-transformer models.
Explore how concept induction heads interact with other known mechanisms like function vectors.
papers.abstract: Prior work on in-context copying has shown the existence of induction heads, which attend to and promote individual tokens during copying. In this work we discover a new type of induction head: concept-level induction heads, which copy entire lexical units instead of individual tokens. Concept induction heads learn to attend to the ends of multi-token words throughout training, working in parallel with token-level induction heads to copy meaningful text. We show that these heads are responsible for semantic tasks like word-level translation, whereas token induction heads are vital for tasks that can only be done verbatim (like copying nonsense tokens). These two "routes" operate independently: we show that ablation of token induction heads causes models to paraphrase where they would otherwise copy verbatim. By patching concept induction head outputs, we find that they contain language-independent word representations that mediate natural language translation, suggesting that LLMs represent abstract word meanings independent of language or form.

papers.title: Localizing Task Recognition and Task Learning in In-Context Learning via Attention Head Analysis
papers.research_question: How do attention heads in large language models mechanistically implement in-context learning, specifically the components of task recognition and task learning?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Task Subspace Logit Attribution (TSLA) to identify attention heads specialized in task recognition and task learning, providing a unified mechanistic account of in-context learning.
papers.conclusion: The TSLA framework successfully localizes TR and TL components to specific attention heads, providing a unified mechanistic explanation of in-context learning.
papers.key_findings:
TR heads and induction heads are highly overlapping and correlated, indicating that induction heads primarily contribute to task recognition.
TR heads attend more to demonstration labels, while TL heads attend more to query tokens.
Ablating TR heads reduces both accuracy and TR ratio, while ablating TL heads reduces accuracy but not TR ratio.
TR heads align hidden states with the task subspace, while TL heads rotate hidden states within the subspace toward the correct label.
The identified TR heads are consistent across tasks, while TL heads are more task-specific.
papers.abstract: We investigate the mechanistic underpinnings of in-context learning (ICL) in large language models by reconciling two dominant perspectives: the component-level analysis of attention heads and the holistic decomposition of ICL into Task Recognition (TR) and Task Learning (TL). We propose a novel framework based on Task Subspace Logit Attribution (TSLA) to identify attention heads specialized in TR and TL, and demonstrate their distinct yet complementary roles. Through correlation analysis, ablation studies, and input perturbations, we show that the identified TR and TL heads independently and effectively capture the TR and TL components of ICL. Using steering experiments with geometric analysis of hidden states, we reveal that TR heads promote task recognition by aligning hidden states with the task subspace, while TL heads rotate hidden states within the subspace toward the correct label to facilitate prediction. We further show how previous findings on ICL mechanisms, including induction heads and task vectors, can be reconciled with our attention-head-level analysis of the TR-TL decomposition. Our framework thus provides a unified and interpretable account of how large language models execute ICL across diverse tasks and settings.

papers.title: The Evolution of Statistical Induction Heads: In-Context Learning Markov Chains
papers.research_question: How does the in-context learning capability emerge in transformers, specifically for learning Markov chains?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the ICL-MC task as a controlled setting to study in-context learning, showing transformers learn 'statistical induction heads' through phase transitions, and that simplicity bias can delay learning the optimal solution.
papers.conclusion: The ICL-MC task provides a useful controlled setting for understanding in-context learning and the emergence of statistical induction heads, revealing that networks pass through discrete incomplete solutions which may affect the speed of learning more complex circuits.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers learn statistical induction heads to optimally solve the in-context Markov chain task.
Learning occurs in phases: an initial uniform phase, a unigram phase, and a final bigram phase with a rapid transition between them.
The model's bias towards simpler (unigram) solutions can slow down the learning of the optimal bigram solution.
The alignment between the transformer's layers is crucial for the phase transition to the correct solution.
During training, positional embeddings develop an alternating pattern, with a bias towards looking back an odd number of tokens.
future_direction: Investigate how the presence of simple incomplete solutions affects the formation of more complex circuits in language modeling and other rich learning settings.
papers.abstract: Large language models have the ability to generate text that mimics patterns in their inputs. We introduce a simple Markov Chain sequence modeling task in order to study how this in-context learning (ICL) capability emerges. In our setting, each example is sampled from a Markov chain drawn from a prior distribution over Markov chains. Transformers trained on this task form \emph{statistical induction heads} which compute accurate next-token probabilities given the bigram statistics of the context. During the course of training, models pass through multiple phases: after an initial stage in which predictions are uniform, they learn to sub-optimally predict using in-context single-token statistics (unigrams); then, there is a rapid phase transition to the correct in-context bigram solution. We conduct an empirical and theoretical investigation of this multi-phase process, showing how successful learning results from the interaction between the transformer's layers, and uncovering evidence that the presence of the simpler unigram solution may delay formation of the final bigram solution. We examine how learning is affected by varying the prior distribution over Markov chains, and consider the generalization of our in-context learning of Markov chains (ICL-MC) task to $n$-grams for $n > 2$.

papers.title: Learning without training: The implicit dynamics of in-context learning
papers.research_question: How does in-context learning in transformers work? The paper investigates whether the context can be seen as implicit weight updates to the MLP layer.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that transformer blocks implicitly transform context into low-rank weight updates of the MLP layer, providing a mechanism for in-context learning.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that in-context learning in transformers can be understood as implicit low-rank weight updates to the MLP layer, connecting ICL to model editing and providing a foundation for prompt engineering.
papers.key_findings:
Theorem 2.2 shows that the effect of context on a contextual block corresponds to a rank-1 weight update of the MLP layer.
Proposition 3.1 shows that the implicit weight updates follow a gradient descent-like dynamics as tokens are processed.
Experiments verify that the implicit weight update formula exactly matches the output with context for linear regression tasks.
The implicit weight updates are highly aligned with weight updates from finetuning via gradient descent.
The framework generalizes to other contextual layers like RNNs, but self-attention leads to more stable convergence.
papers.limitation: The implicit weight updates depend on the specific query token, so the context cannot be exactly represented by a single fixed weight update for all inputs.
future_direction: Unifying ICL with model editing by connecting steering vectors and rank-1 edits to the same mechanism.
Developing a formal theory of prompt engineering based on the algebraic properties of the implicit weight updates.
Investigating whether token-dependent updates can be aggregated into static approximations for prompt compression.
papers.abstract: One of the most striking features of Large Language Models (LLMs) is their ability to learn in-context. Namely at inference time an LLM is able to learn new patterns without any additional weight update when these patterns are presented in the form of examples in the prompt, even if these patterns were not seen during training. The mechanisms through which this can happen are still largely unknown. In this work, we show that the stacking of a self-attention layer with an MLP, allows the transformer block to implicitly modify the weights of the MLP layer according to the context. We argue through theory and experimentation that this simple mechanism may be the reason why LLMs can learn in-context and not only during training. Specifically, we show how a transformer block implicitly transforms a context into a low-rank weight-update of its MLP layer.

papers.title: Task Vectors, Learned Not Extracted: Performance Gains and Mechanistic Insight
papers.research_question: How can we obtain effective task vectors for in-context learning, and what are the mechanisms by which they influence model predictions?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Learned Task Vectors (LTVs), which are directly trained and outperform extracted task vectors, and provides a mechanistic analysis showing that task vectors primarily act through attention-head OV circuits and propagate linearly through subsequent layers.
papers.conclusion: LTVs provide an efficient and flexible method for obtaining effective task vectors and offer a principled lens into the mechanistic foundations of in-context learning.
papers.key_findings:
LTVs consistently outperform extracted task vectors (Vanilla TV and Function Vector) and match or exceed in-context learning performance across multiple models and tasks.
LTVs are flexible and can be effectively injected at arbitrary layers, token positions, and even into in-context learning prompts.
The low-level mechanism of task vectors involves interaction with attention-head OV circuits, with a small subset of 'key heads' being most decisive.
Despite Transformer nonlinearities, the propagation of injected task vectors through subsequent layers is largely linear, characterized by rotation toward task-relevant subspaces in early layers and scaling in magnitude in later layers.
Task vectors exhibit compositionality and cross-task generalization that is constrained by overlap in the label space of tasks.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) can perform new tasks from in-context demonstrations, a phenomenon known as in-context learning (ICL). Recent work suggests that these demonstrations are compressed into task vectors (TVs), compact task representations that LLMs exploit for predictions. However, prior studies typically extract TVs from model outputs or hidden states using cumbersome and opaque methods, and they rarely elucidate the mechanisms by which TVs influence computation. In this work, we address both limitations. First, we propose directly training Learned Task Vectors (LTVs), which surpass extracted TVs in accuracy and exhibit superior flexibility-acting effectively at arbitrary layers, positions, and even with ICL prompts. Second, through systematic analysis, we investigate the mechanistic role of TVs, showing that at the low level they steer predictions primarily through attention-head OV circuits, with a small subset of "key heads" most decisive. At a higher level, we find that despite Transformer nonlinearities, TV propagation is largely linear: early TVs are rotated toward task-relevant subspaces to improve logits of relevant labels, while later TVs are predominantly scaled in magnitude. Taken together, LTVs not only provide a practical approach for obtaining effective TVs but also offer a principled lens into the mechanistic foundations of ICL.

papers.title: Mechanism of Task-oriented Information Removal in In-context Learning
papers.research_question: What is the inner mechanism of in-context learning, and how does task-oriented information removal play a role?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes that in-context learning works by removing task-irrelevant information from the query's hidden states, and identifies Denoising Heads as the attention heads responsible for this removal.
papers.conclusion: Task-oriented information removal is a key mechanism in in-context learning, and Denoising Heads play a causal role in this process.
papers.key_findings:
Zero-shot queries are encoded into non-selective representations containing information for all possible tasks, leading to arbitrary outputs.
Injecting a low-rank filter (Task-Verbalization Subspace) that removes task-irrelevant information from zero-shot hidden states can steer the model to the correct task and improve accuracy.
Few-shot ICL implicitly performs task-oriented information removal, as measured by increased eccentricity and covariance flux in the hidden states, aligning them with the Task-Verbalization Subspace.
Denoising Heads are identified as attention heads that contribute to information removal; ablating them reduces ICL accuracy, especially in unseen label scenarios.
The information removal mechanism is distinct from and complements induction heads, and is critical for ICL when the correct label is absent from demonstrations.
papers.abstract: In-context Learning (ICL) is an emerging few-shot learning paradigm based on modern Language Models (LMs), yet its inner mechanism remains unclear. In this paper, we investigate the mechanism through a novel perspective of information removal. Specifically, we demonstrate that in the zero-shot scenario, LMs encode queries into non-selective representations in hidden states containing information for all possible tasks, leading to arbitrary outputs without focusing on the intended task, resulting in near-zero accuracy. Meanwhile, we find that selectively removing specific information from hidden states by a low-rank filter effectively steers LMs toward the intended task. Building on these findings, by measuring the hidden states on carefully designed metrics, we observe that few-shot ICL effectively simulates such task-oriented information removal processes, selectively removing the redundant information from entangled non-selective representations, and improving the output based on the demonstrations, which constitutes a key mechanism underlying ICL. Moreover, we identify essential attention heads inducing the removal operation, termed Denoising Heads, which enables the ablation experiments blocking the information removal operation from the inference, where the ICL accuracy significantly degrades, especially when the correct label is absent from the few-shot demonstrations, confirming both the critical role of the information removal mechanism and denoising heads.

papers.title: What In-Context Learning "Learns" In-Context: Disentangling Task Recognition and Task Learning
papers.research_question: How does in-context learning (ICL) work in large language models, and can the contributions of task recognition (applying pre-trained priors) and task learning (acquiring new input-label mappings) be disentangled?
papers.core_contribution: The paper disentangles in-context learning into task recognition (TR) and task learning (TL), showing TR is present across model scales but does not improve with larger models or more demonstrations, while TL is an emergent ability that scales with model size and benefits from more demonstrations.
papers.conclusion: In-context learning comprises two distinct phenomena—task recognition and task learning—which emerge under different conditions; TR is a broad capability that doesn't scale, while TL is an emergent ability of large models that improves with scale and demonstrations.
papers.key_findings:
Task recognition enables non-trivial performance even with small models and few demonstrations, but its performance does not scale with model size or number of demonstrations.
Task learning emerges with larger model scales, and its performance consistently improves with more in-context demonstrations.
The performance gap between standard ICL (GOLD) and the TR-only setting (RANDOM) grows with larger models, indicating an increasing role for TL at scale.
With the largest models and sufficient demonstrations, models can learn novel mappings to abstract labels (TL) and sometimes match the performance of standard ICL.
Task difficulty affects the scaling trends, with simpler tasks (e.g., sentiment analysis) showing better TL scaling than harder tasks (e.g., natural language inference).
papers.limitation:
The work is limited to classification tasks because they are easier to adapt to the experimental setups (RANDOM and ABSTRACT).
The mechanistic understanding of how models perform 'task learning' (e.g., whether it's implicit gradient descent or an advanced form of recognition) remains elusive.
future_direction: Future work on ICL should distinguish between the two phenomena (TR and TL) and clearly state the experimental conditions.
Extending the investigation to other types of NLP tasks beyond classification.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exploit in-context learning (ICL) to solve tasks with only a few demonstrations, but its mechanisms are not yet well-understood. Some works suggest that LLMs only recall already learned concepts from pre-training, while others hint that ICL performs implicit learning over demonstrations. We characterize two ways through which ICL leverages demonstrations. Task recognition (TR) captures the extent to which LLMs can recognize a task through demonstrations -- even without ground-truth labels -- and apply their pre-trained priors, whereas task learning (TL) is the ability to capture new input-label mappings unseen in pre-training. Using a wide range of classification datasets and three LLM families (GPT-3, LLaMA and OPT), we design controlled experiments to disentangle the roles of TR and TL in ICL. We show that (1) models can achieve non-trivial performance with only TR, and TR does not further improve with larger models or more demonstrations; (2) LLMs acquire TL as the model scales, and TL's performance consistently improves with more demonstrations in context. Our findings unravel two different forces behind ICL and we advocate for discriminating them in future ICL research due to their distinct nature.

papers.title: Unveiling In-Context Learning: A Coordinate System to Understand Its Working Mechanism
papers.research_question: What is the underlying working mechanism of in-context learning (ICL) in large language models? The paper aims to unify two conflicting views: one emphasizing the impact of similar examples and the other attributing ICL to task recognition.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a two-dimensional coordinate system that unifies two conflicting views on in-context learning (ICL), explaining ICL behavior through two orthogonal variables: perception (whether similar examples are present) and cognition (whether the model can recognize the task).
papers.conclusion: The proposed two-dimensional coordinate system provides a principled and universal framework to understand the working mechanism of in-context learning in large language models.
papers.key_findings:
In the first quadrant (task recognized, similar examples present), models leverage both pre-trained knowledge and similar examples. If labels of similar examples are incorrect, smaller models tend to replicate incorrect labels while larger models rely more on pre-trained knowledge.
In the second quadrant (task recognized, no similar examples), models primarily use pre-trained knowledge and increasing the number of demonstration shots does not significantly improve performance.
In the third quadrant (task not recognized, no similar examples), ICL fails and models tend to predict the label of the first example due to positional bias.
In the fourth quadrant (task not recognized, similar examples present), models directly copy the labels of similar examples, and larger models are better at recognizing similar examples, increasing copying tendency.
The coordinate system explains the conflicting effects of label correctness and shot number: label correctness matters when similar examples are present, and shot number helps by increasing the chance of including similar examples.
papers.limitation:
The coordinate system is primarily validated on classification tasks, with only a brief case study on generation tasks.
The study is limited to models with up to 40B parameters.
future_direction: Extend the coordinate system to more generation tasks.
Apply the coordinate system to larger models (beyond 40B parameters).
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit remarkable in-context learning (ICL) capabilities. However, the underlying working mechanism of ICL remains poorly understood. Recent research presents two conflicting views on ICL: One emphasizes the impact of similar examples in the demonstrations, stressing the need for label correctness and more shots. The other attributes it to LLMs' inherent ability of task recognition, deeming label correctness and shot numbers of demonstrations as not crucial. In this work, we provide a Two-Dimensional Coordinate System that unifies both views into a systematic framework. The framework explains the behavior of ICL through two orthogonal variables: whether similar examples are presented in the demonstrations (perception) and whether LLMs can recognize the task (cognition). We propose the peak inverse rank metric to detect the task recognition ability of LLMs and study LLMs' reactions to different definitions of similarity. Based on these, we conduct extensive experiments to elucidate how ICL functions across each quadrant on multiple representative classification tasks. Finally, we extend our analyses to generation tasks, showing that our coordinate system can also be used to interpret ICL for generation tasks effectively.

papers.title: Scaling Laws and Interpretability of Learning from Repeated Data
papers.research_question: What are the effects of repeated data on language model training, and how does it mechanistically affect model components like induction heads?
papers.core_contribution: Repeated data causes a double-descent phenomenon in language models, leading to severe performance degradation that is mechanistically linked to disproportionate damage to induction heads and copying mechanisms, shifting the model from generalization to memorization.
papers.conclusion: Small fractions of repeated data, if repeated at a specific frequency, can cause surprisingly severe performance degradation in language models, and this degradation is associated with disproportionate damage to internal mechanisms like induction heads that support generalization.
papers.key_findings:
Repeated data induces a strong double-descent phenomenon, with a predictable range of repetition frequency causing severe performance degradation.
A small fraction of repeated data (e.g., 0.1% repeated 100 times) can degrade an 800M parameter model's performance to that of a 400M parameter model.
Repeated data disproportionately damages copying ability and induction heads, which are internal structures associated with generalization.
The damage to induction heads provides a mechanistic explanation for the shift from generalization to memorization.
The double-descent phenomenon and associated performance degradation are also observed when training on Python code data.
papers.abstract: Recent large language models have been trained on vast datasets, but also often on repeated data, either intentionally for the purpose of upweighting higher quality data, or unintentionally because data deduplication is not perfect and the model is exposed to repeated data at the sentence, paragraph, or document level. Some works have reported substantial negative performance effects of this repeated data. In this paper we attempt to study repeated data systematically and to understand its effects mechanistically. To do this, we train a family of models where most of the data is unique but a small fraction of it is repeated many times. We find a strong double descent phenomenon, in which repeated data can lead test loss to increase midway through training. A predictable range of repetition frequency leads to surprisingly severe degradation in performance. For instance, performance of an 800M parameter model can be degraded to that of a 2x smaller model (400M params) by repeating 0.1% of the data 100 times, despite the other 90% of the training tokens remaining unique. We suspect there is a range in the middle where the data can be memorized and doing so consumes a large fraction of the model's capacity, and this may be where the peak of degradation occurs. Finally, we connect these observations to recent mechanistic interpretability work - attempting to reverse engineer the detailed computations performed by the model - by showing that data repetition disproportionately damages copying and internal structures associated with generalization, such as induction heads, providing a possible mechanism for the shift from generalization to memorization. Taken together, these results provide a hypothesis for why repeating a relatively small fraction of data in large language models could lead to disproportionately large harms to performance.

papers.title: Language Models "Grok" to Copy
papers.research_question: How do language models develop context copying abilities during pre-training, and is this process similar to grokking?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes that language models develop context copying abilities through a process similar to grokking, with evidence from pre-training dynamics.
papers.conclusion: The development of context copying in language models is a form of grokking, offering insights for improving language model training and in-context performance.
