papers.key_findings:
Pre-training loss decreases rapidly while context copying ability lags and then abruptly saturates, resembling grokking.
The development of copying ability is independent of the number of tokens trained, similar to grokking speed.
Induction heads form from shallow to deep layers during training, mirroring circuit development in grokking.
Regularization techniques like dropout and weight decay can accelerate or enhance the development of context copying.
papers.limitation: The study focuses on copying tasks and does not evaluate in-context learning (ICL) tasks, which are more complex, due to limited computational resources.
future_direction: Applying the understanding of grokking to improve in-context capacities like ICL in language models.
papers.abstract: We examine the pre-training dynamics of language models, focusing on their ability to copy text from preceding context--a fundamental skill for various LLM applications, including in-context learning (ICL) and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). We propose a novel perspective that Transformer-based language models develop copying abilities similarly to grokking, which refers to sudden generalization on test set long after the model fit to the training set. Our experiments yield three arguments: (1) The pre-training loss decreases rapidly, while the context copying ability of models initially lags and then abruptly saturates. (2) The speed of developing copying ability is independent of the number of tokens trained, similarly to how grokking speed is unaffected by dataset size as long as the data distribution is preserved. (3) Induction heads, the attention heads responsible for copying, form from shallow to deep layers during training, mirroring the development of circuits in deeper layers during grokking. We contend that the connection between grokking and context copying can provide valuable insights for more effective language model training, ultimately improving in-context performance. For example, we demonstrated that techniques that enhance grokking, such as regularization, either accelerate or enhance the development of context copying.

papers.title: Linguistic Neuron Overlap Patterns to Facilitate Cross-lingual Transfer on Low-resource Languages
papers.research_question: How can we improve cross-lingual capabilities of LLMs on low-resource languages by selecting an optimal bridge language in Cross-lingual In-Context Learning (X-ICL), and whether sharing neurons can facilitate cross-lingual transfer?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes BridgeX-ICL, a method to improve zero-shot cross-lingual in-context learning for low-resource languages by selecting an optimal bridge language based on neuron overlap patterns and an HSIC-based similarity metric.
papers.conclusion: Explores whether sharing neurons can improve LLMs' cross-lingual performance on low-resource languages and proposes BridgeX-ICL, a language-bridge approach validated on multiple cross-lingual tasks and language pairs.
papers.key_findings:
Strong neural overlaps align with human linguistic taxonomy within language families, but do not consistently hold across families.
Overlapping neurons embody shared semantic information, regardless of the language within or between families.
BridgeX-ICL improves performance on cross-lingual tasks (BLI and MRC) across 15 language pairs by an average of 6.02% and 5.25% over zero-shot baselines.
English is selected as the optimal bridge in 9 out of 15 language pairs in LLaMA (7 out of 15 in Mistral), indicating high-resource, Latin-script languages tend to be the default bridge, but non-Latin script languages like Chinese also show potential.
papers.limitation:
Limited coverage of language pairs and tasks due to lack of comprehensive benchmarks for low-resource languages.
The proposed linguistic distance measurement is probe-data-induced, offering qualitative but not quantitative insights.
Bridge selection reflects training biases of LLMs, inevitably reflecting their training data distribution.
papers.abstract:
The current Large Language Models (LLMs) face significant challenges in improving their
performance on low-resource languages and urgently need data-efficient methods without
costly fine-tuning. From the perspective of language-bridge, we propose a simple yet effective method, namely BridgeXICL,
to improve the zero-shot Cross-lingual In-Context Learning (X-ICL) for low-resource languages. Unlike existing works focusing on
language-specific neurons, BridgeX-ICL explores whether sharing neurons can improve
cross-lingual performance in LLMs. We construct neuron probe data from the groundtruth
MUSE bilingual dictionaries, and define a subset of language overlap neurons accordingly to ensure full activation of these anchored
neurons. Subsequently, we propose
an HSIC-based metric to quantify LLMs’ internal linguistic spectrum based on overlapping neurons, guiding optimal bridge selection.
The experiments conducted on 4 crosslingual tasks and 15 language pairs from 7 diverse families, covering both high-low and moderate-low pairs, validate the effectiveness of BridgeX-ICL and offer empirical insights into the underlying multilingual mechanisms of LLMs. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/
xuyuemei/BridgeX-ICL.

papers.title: Analyzing Context Contributions in LLM-based Machine Translation
papers.research_question: How do large language models (LLMs) use different parts of the input context, such as few-shot examples and the source text, when generating translations in machine translation (MT)?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a comprehensive analysis of context utilization in LLM-based machine translation, revealing how different parts of the input context contribute to the generated translation, including positional biases and the impact of task-specific training.
papers.conclusion: The analysis sheds light on the internal workings of LLM-based machine translation, revealing contribution patterns and positional biases that differ from standard encoder-decoder MT models.
papers.key_findings:
The source part of few-shot examples contributes more than its corresponding target, irrespective of translation direction.
Training on parallel data (fine-tuning or continued pretraining) reduces the influence of few-shot examples on the translated sequence.
There is a positional bias where earlier few-shot examples have higher contributions to the translated sequence, and this bias is maintained across different generation stages.
Low source contributions can potentially uncover pathological translations, such as hallucinations.
The relative ranking of context parts' contributions remains stable throughout the generation process, with the source text consistently having the highest contribution.
papers.limitation: Due to high GPU memory requirements, samples with large context length had to be filtered, limiting the analysis to shorter sequences.
future_direction: Exploring how to train dedicated models to be better guided by in-context examples.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved state-of-the-art performance in machine translation (MT) and demonstrated the ability to leverage in-context learning through few-shot examples. However, the mechanisms by which LLMs use different parts of the input context remain largely unexplored. In this work, we provide a comprehensive analysis of context utilization in MT, studying how LLMs use various context parts, such as few-shot examples and the source text, when generating translations. We highlight several key findings: (1) the source part of few-shot examples appears to contribute more than its corresponding targets, irrespective of translation direction; (2) finetuning LLMs with parallel data alters the contribution patterns of different context parts; and (3) there is a positional bias where earlier few-shot examples have higher contributions to the translated sequence. Finally, we demonstrate that inspecting anomalous context contributions can potentially uncover pathological translations, such as hallucinations. Our findings shed light on the internal workings of LLM-based MT which go beyond those known for standard encoder-decoder MT models.

papers.title: Interactive Visualization and Manipulation of Attention-based Neural Machine Translation
papers.research_question: How can we interpret and analyze the behavior of neural machine translation, specifically focusing on beam search and attention components?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces an interactive web-based tool for visualizing and manipulating neural machine translation behavior, specifically focusing on beam search and attention mechanisms, to help users understand NMT.
papers.conclusion: The proposed interactive tool provides methods to visualize and manipulate NMT, aiding in the understanding of its behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Visualizing beam search as a tree helps understand how hypotheses are selected and discarded during decoding.
Manual adjustment of attention weights allows users to see how specific source words influence target token probabilities.
Automatic adjustment of attention weights to maximize output probability can make attention alignments more interpretable.
The tool enables exploration of hypotheses not covered by beam search by manually expanding nodes.
Attention weights in NMT may not always look like clear alignments due to language ordering differences, but adjustment can clarify them.
papers.abstract: While neural machine translation (NMT) provides high-quality translation, it is still hard to interpret and analyze its behavior. We present an interactive interface for visualizing and intervening behavior of NMT, specifically concentrating on the behavior of beam search mechanism and attention component. The tool (1) visualizes search tree and attention and (2) provides interface to adjust search tree and attention weight (manually or automatically) at real-time. We show the tool help users understand NMT in various ways.

papers.title: An Explanation of In-context Learning as Implicit Bayesian Inference
papers.research_question: What enables in-context learning in language models? The paper studies how in-context learning can emerge when pretraining documents have long-range coherence.
papers.core_contribution: In-context learning can be explained as implicit Bayesian inference when pretraining data has long-range coherence, proven in a mixture of HMMs setting and validated with experiments on a synthetic dataset.
papers.conclusion: In-context learning can be cast as implicit Bayesian inference, providing a first step towards understanding in-context learning and insight for improving pretraining and prompting.
papers.key_findings:
In-context learning emerges when pretraining documents have long-range coherence and the model infers a latent concept shared across examples.
Theoretical analysis shows that in-context learning error decreases with the number of examples and example length.
Experiments on the synthetic dataset GINC show that both Transformers and LSTMs exhibit in-context learning.
In-context accuracy improves with model scaling despite achieving the same pretraining loss.
In-context learning is sensitive to example order, and zero-shot can sometimes be better than few-shot.
papers.limitation:
The theory assumes the language model fits the pretraining distribution exactly, which may not hold in practice.
The synthetic dataset GINC is simple compared to real-world data.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to variable example lengths.
Bridging the mismatch between training and test example lengths.
Analyzing the effect of model scaling and architecture.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LMs) such as GPT-3 have the surprising ability to do in-context learning, where the model learns to do a downstream task simply by conditioning on a prompt consisting of input-output examples. The LM learns from these examples without being explicitly pretrained to learn. Thus, it is unclear what enables in-context learning. In this paper, we study how in-context learning can emerge when pretraining documents have long-range coherence. Here, the LM must infer a latent document-level concept to generate coherent next tokens during pretraining. At test time, in-context learning occurs when the LM also infers a shared latent concept between examples in a prompt. We prove when this occurs despite a distribution mismatch between prompts and pretraining data in a setting where the pretraining distribution is a mixture of HMMs. In contrast to messy large-scale datasets used to train LMs capable of in-context learning, we generate a small-scale synthetic dataset (GINC) where Transformers and LSTMs both exhibit in-context learning. Beyond the theory, experiments on GINC exhibit large-scale real-world phenomena including improved in-context performance with model scaling (despite the same pretraining loss), sensitivity to example order, and instances where zero-shot is better than few-shot in-context learning.

papers.title: In-context Vectors: Making In Context Learning More Effective and Controllable Through Latent Space Steering
papers.research_question: How can in-context learning be made more effective and controllable through latent space steering?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes In-Context Vectors (ICV), an inference-only method that recasts in-context learning as latent space steering, making it more effective, controllable, and efficient than standard ICL and fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: ICV improves the effectiveness and efficiency of in-context learning, enabling LLMs to adapt to tasks without fine-tuning and combine multiple tasks through vector arithmetic.
papers.key_findings:
ICV outperforms standard in-context learning and LoRA fine-tuning on diverse tasks including language detoxification, style transfer, and role-playing.
The strength of ICV can be controlled by adjusting the scaling factor λ, allowing trade-offs between task adherence and semantic preservation.
ICV benefits from more demonstration examples, similar to ICL, but without context length constraints.
ICV is most effective when applied to all layers of the transformer, rather than individual layers.
ICV enables task arithmetic, allowing multiple tasks to be combined through vector addition and negation.
papers.limitation: ICV requires access to the model to add the in-context vector, which is easy for open-source models but may be a constraint for closed models.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) demonstrate emergent in-context learning capabilities, where they adapt to new tasks based on example demonstrations. However, in-context learning has seen limited effectiveness in many settings, is difficult to quantitatively control and takes up context window space. To overcome these limitations, we propose an alternative approach that recasts in-context learning as in-context vectors (ICV). Using ICV has two steps. We first use a forward pass on demonstration examples to create the in-context vector from the latent embedding of the LLM. This vector captures essential information about the intended task. On a new query, instead of adding demonstrations to the prompt, we shift the latent states of the LLM using the ICV. The ICV approach has several benefits: 1) it enables the LLM to more effectively follow the demonstration examples; 2) it's easy to control by adjusting the magnitude of the ICV; 3) it reduces the length of the prompt by removing the in-context demonstrations; 4) ICV is computationally much more efficient than fine-tuning. We demonstrate that ICV achieves better performance compared to standard in-context learning and fine-tuning on diverse tasks including safety, style transfer, role-playing and formatting. Moreover, we show that we can flexibly teach LLM to simultaneously follow different types of instructions by simple vector arithmetics on the corresponding ICVs.

papers.title: Disentangling meaning from language in LLM-based machine translation
papers.research_question: How do LLMs internally encode and distribute translation functions, specifically target language identification and sentence equivalence, at the sentence level?
papers.core_contribution: Translation in LLMs is implemented by sparse, distinct sets of attention heads for target language identification and sentence equivalence; steering these heads enables instruction-free machine translation performance comparable to instruction-based prompting.
papers.conclusion: Translation in LLMs is implemented by sparse, specialized attention heads for language and equivalence, and these representations are transferable and can be steered to control translation behavior.
papers.key_findings:
A small subset of attention heads (≈1%) play a considerable role in MT performance across all pairs, demonstrating that translation is mechanistically localized.
Target language identification and sentence equivalence are encoded by distinct, separable sets of heads.
This organization holds across 20 translation directions.
Steering vectors built from these heads enable instruction-free MT performance comparable to instruction-based prompting.
Ablating these heads selectively disrupts their corresponding translation functions.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic Interpretability (MI) seeks to explain how neural networks implement their capabilities, but the scale of Large Language Models (LLMs) has limited prior MI work in Machine Translation (MT) to word-level analyses. We study sentence-level MT from a mechanistic perspective by analyzing attention heads to understand how LLMs internally encode and distribute translation functions. We decompose MT into two subtasks: producing text in the target language (i.e. target language identification) and preserving the input sentence's meaning (i.e. sentence equivalence). Across three families of open-source models and 20 translation directions, we find that distinct, sparse sets of attention heads specialize in each subtask. Based on this insight, we construct subtask-specific steering vectors and show that modifying just 1% of the relevant heads enables instruction-free MT performance comparable to instruction-based prompting, while ablating these heads selectively disrupts their corresponding translation functions.

papers.title: Finding the Translation Switch: Discovering and Exploiting the Task-Initiation Features in LLMs
papers.research_question: What internal mechanism within instruction-tuned models is responsible for the innate translation ability of LLMs?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a framework to identify 'translation initiation' features in LLMs using Sparse Autoencoders and demonstrates their causal role; proposes a mechanistic data selection strategy for efficient fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: The paper decodes the translation initiation features in LLMs and shows how mechanistic insights can be used for efficient fine-tuning and specialization.
papers.key_findings:
A small set of 'translation initiation' features are causally responsible for the model's translation ability.
Amplifying these features improves translation quality and reduces hallucinations across diverse language pairs.
These features are language-agnostic and generalize across different translation directions.
A data selection strategy that prioritizes 'mechanistically hard' samples (low activation of initiation features) improves fine-tuning efficiency and reduces hallucinations.
The identified mechanisms are transferable across scales within the same model family but not across different architectures.
papers.limitation: The translation initiation features are not transferable across different model architectures.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) frequently exhibit strong translation abilities, even without task-specific fine-tuning. However, the internal mechanisms governing this innate capability remain largely opaque. To demystify this process, we leverage Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) and introduce a novel framework for identifying task-specific features. Our method first recalls features that are frequently co-activated on translation inputs and then filters them for functional coherence using a PCA-based consistency metric. This framework successfully isolates a small set of **translation initiation** features. Causal interventions demonstrate that amplifying these features steers the model towards correct translation, while ablating them induces hallucinations and off-task outputs, confirming they represent a core component of the model's innate translation competency. Moving from analysis to application, we leverage this mechanistic insight to propose a new data selection strategy for efficient fine-tuning. Specifically, we prioritize training on **mechanistically hard** samples-those that fail to naturally activate the translation initiation features. Experiments show this approach significantly improves data efficiency and suppresses hallucinations. Furthermore, we find these mechanisms are transferable to larger models of the same family. Our work not only decodes a core component of the translation mechanism in LLMs but also provides a blueprint for using internal model mechanism to create more robust and efficient models. The codes are available at https://github.com/flamewei123/AAAI26-translation-Initiation-Features.

papers.title: Understanding In-Context Learning via Supportive Pretraining Data
papers.research_question: What makes certain pretraining data supportive for in-context learning, and what are the characteristics of such data?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a gradient-based method (ORCA-ICL) to identify a small subset of pretraining data that supports in-context learning and analyzes the characteristics of this supportive data.
papers.conclusion: The work takes a first step towards understanding in-context learning by analyzing instance-level pretraining data, and the findings may guide future pretraining data construction to actively improve models' in-context learning performance.
papers.key_findings:
The supportive pretraining data for in-context learning do not have a higher domain relevance to downstream tasks compared to random pretraining data.
The supportive pretraining data contain a relatively higher mass of rarely occurring, long-tail tokens.
The supportive pretraining data are challenging examples where the information gain from incorporating long-range context is below average, indicating that learning to incorporate difficult long-range context encourages in-context learning.
A continued pretraining on the identified supportive subset significantly improves the model's in-context learning ability, by up to 18%, without improving zero-shot performance.
The cross-task effectiveness of the supportive data suggests that part of the in-context learning behavior is task-specific and not universal across tasks.
papers.limitation:
The supportive pretraining data are identified with respect to the current language model checkpoint, and early checkpoints might have different supportive data.
The ORCA-ICL method is computationally expensive due to its gradient-based nature and the large size of pretraining data.
future_direction: Convert the correlational findings to causal ones to actively refine or construct pretraining data for improved in-context learning.
Apply the ORCA-ICL method to generation tasks in addition to classification tasks.
papers.abstract: In-context learning (ICL) improves language models' performance on a variety of NLP tasks by simply demonstrating a handful of examples at inference time. It is not well understood why ICL ability emerges, as the model has never been specifically trained on such demonstrations. Unlike prior work that explores implicit mechanisms behind ICL, we study ICL via investigating the pretraining data. Specifically, we first adapt an iterative, gradient-based approach to find a small subset of pretraining data that supports ICL. We observe that a continued pretraining on this small subset significantly improves the model's ICL ability, by up to 18%. We then compare the supportive subset constrastively with random subsets of pretraining data and discover: (1) The supportive pretraining data to ICL do not have a higher domain relevance to downstream tasks. (2) The supportive pretraining data have a higher mass of rarely occurring, long-tail tokens. (3) The supportive pretraining data are challenging examples where the information gain from long-range context is below average, indicating learning to incorporate difficult long-range context encourages ICL. Our work takes a first step towards understanding ICL via analyzing instance-level pretraining data. Our insights have a potential to enhance the ICL ability of language models by actively guiding the construction of pretraining data in the future.

papers.title: Is attention required for ICL? Exploring the Relationship Between Model Architecture and In-Context Learning Ability
papers.research_question: What is the relationship between model architecture and in-context learning ability? Which architectures are capable of ICL and which exhibit superior performance?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that in-context learning is not exclusive to attention-based models; all tested architectures can perform ICL, with some attention alternatives being competitive with or better than transformers in certain tasks.
papers.conclusion: In-context learning is not exclusive to attention-based models; all tested architectures can perform ICL, with attention alternatives being competitive. However, no architecture is consistent across all tasks, and performance degrades with out-of-distribution prompt lengths.
papers.key_findings:
All considered architectures can perform in-context learning, demonstrating ICL is not exclusive to attention-based models.
Attention alternatives such as Mamba, Hyena, RetNet, and RWKV are sometimes competitive with or better than transformers at ICL.
Performance varies with number of in-context examples; some architectures show degradation when extrapolating to longer prompts than seen in training.
The emergence of ICL in image classification is influenced by burstiness in training data; some architectures are predisposed towards memorization over ICL.
ICL score in language modeling correlates with performance on other ICL tasks, but not perfectly.
papers.abstract: What is the relationship between model architecture and the ability to perform in-context learning? In this empirical study, we take the first steps toward answering this question. We evaluate thirteen model architectures capable of causal language modeling across a suite of synthetic in-context learning tasks. These selected architectures represent a broad range of paradigms, including recurrent and convolution-based neural networks, transformers, state space model inspired, and other emerging attention alternatives. We discover that all the considered architectures can perform in-context learning under a wider range of conditions than previously documented. Additionally, we observe stark differences in statistical efficiency and consistency by varying the number of in-context examples and task difficulty. We also measure each architecture's predisposition towards in-context learning when presented with the option to memorize rather than leverage in-context examples. Finally, and somewhat surprisingly, we find that several attention alternatives are sometimes competitive with or better in-context learners than transformers. However, no single architecture demonstrates consistency across all tasks, with performance either plateauing or declining when confronted with a significantly larger number of in-context examples than those encountered during gradient-based training.

papers.title: Learning Task Representations from In-Context Learning
papers.research_question: How can we develop a task representation that generalizes across modalities like language and mathematical functions, and how can this representation be leveraged to preserve task fidelity on downstream tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an automated method to encode in-context learning tasks as a weighted sum of attention heads (Learnable Task Vector), which generalizes effectively across text and functional regression modalities.
papers.conclusion: The Learnable Task Vector provides a principled, automated, and modality-agnostic method for representing in-context learning tasks, demonstrating strong generalization across text and regression domains.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed Learnable Task Vector (LTV) preserves task information in out-of-distribution (OOD) cases where existing methods fail.
LTV's performance benefits stem from effective task encoding, not from fine-tuning the backbone model.
LTV aligns the distribution of the last hidden state with that of an optimally in-context-learned model, providing insight into task steering.
LTV outperforms existing task vector methods (Function Vector, In-Context Vector) on both regression and language tasks.
LTV requires only a small extension beyond the training sequence length to generalize effectively.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable proficiency in in-context learning (ICL), where models adapt to new tasks through example-based prompts without requiring parameter updates. However, understanding how tasks are internally encoded and generalized remains a challenge. To address some of the empirical and technical gaps in the literature, we introduce an automated formulation for encoding task information in ICL prompts as a function of attention heads within the transformer architecture. This approach computes a single task vector as a weighted sum of attention heads, with the weights optimized causally via gradient descent. Our findings show that existing methods fail to generalize effectively to modalities beyond text. In response, we also design a benchmark to evaluate whether a task vector can preserve task fidelity in functional regression tasks. The proposed method successfully extracts task-specific information from in-context demonstrations and excels in both text and regression tasks, demonstrating its generalizability across modalities.

papers.title: The representation landscape of few-shot learning and fine-tuning in large language models
papers.research_question: How do in-context learning (ICL) and supervised fine-tuning (SFT) affect the geometry of the internal representations in large language models when solving the same question-answering task?
papers.core_contribution: ICL and SFT create very different internal representation structures in LLMs for the same task, with ICL forming semantically organized clusters in early layers and SFT forming sharper answer-encoding clusters in later layers.
papers.conclusion: Geometric analysis reveals a transition between layers encoding high-level semantic information and those generating answers, showing fine-tuning and few-shot learning take distinct approaches to extract information from LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Both few-shot learning and fine-tuning show a clear division between model layers, with a marked peak in intrinsic dimension and a sudden change in geometrical structure in the middle of the network.
Few-shot learning leads to semantically meaningful clustering of representations in early layers, organized hierarchically by subject.
Fine-tuning enhances the sharp emergence of clustered representations according to answer identity in the second half of the network.
The representation landscape of ICL is more interpretable in early layers, while SFT is fuzzier in early layers but develops better-defined answer-encoding peaks later.
The transition layer separates layers encoding high-level semantics from those involved in generating answers.
papers.abstract: In-context learning (ICL) and supervised fine-tuning (SFT) are two common strategies for improving the performance of modern large language models (LLMs) on specific tasks. Despite their different natures, these strategies often lead to comparable performance gains. However, little is known about whether they induce similar representations inside LLMs. We approach this problem by analyzing the probability landscape of their hidden representations in the two cases. More specifically, we compare how LLMs solve the same question-answering task, finding that ICL and SFT create very different internal structures, in both cases undergoing a sharp transition in the middle of the network. In the first half of the network, ICL shapes interpretable representations hierarchically organized according to their semantic content. In contrast, the probability landscape obtained with SFT is fuzzier and semantically mixed. In the second half of the model, the fine-tuned representations develop probability modes that better encode the identity of answers, while the landscape of ICL representations is characterized by less defined peaks. Our approach reveals the diverse computational strategies developed inside LLMs to solve the same task across different conditions, allowing us to make a step towards designing optimal methods to extract information from language models.

papers.title: Everything Everywhere All at Once: LLMs can In-Context Learn Multiple Tasks in Superposition
papers.research_question: Can LLMs perform multiple distinct in-context learning tasks simultaneously in a single inference call (task superposition)?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs can perform multiple distinct in-context learning tasks simultaneously in a single inference call (task superposition), and this capability emerges even when trained on one task at a time.
papers.conclusion: Task superposition is the ability of LLMs to simultaneously solve distinct tasks from in-context examples, present in various pretrained models and improves with model size, with evidence that models internally mix task vectors.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs can in-context learn multiple tasks in superposition when provided with prompts of a mixture of task examples.
Transformers can in-context learn multiple tasks in superposition even if trained to in-context learn one task at a time.
LLMs internally combine task vectors during task superposition.
Convex combinations of task vectors produce task superposition.
Larger models can solve more tasks in parallel and better calibrate their output distribution.
papers.limitation: Conventional decoding algorithms lead to generation collapse, limiting practical application of task superposition.
future_direction: Developing decoding strategies to maintain multi-task state throughout generation.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable in-context learning (ICL) capabilities. In this study, we explore a surprising phenomenon related to ICL: LLMs can perform multiple, computationally distinct ICL tasks simultaneously, during a single inference call, a capability we term "task superposition". We provide empirical evidence of this phenomenon across various LLM families and scales and show that this phenomenon emerges even if we train the model to in-context learn one task at a time. We offer theoretical explanations that this capability is well within the expressive power of transformers. We also explore how LLMs internally compose task vectors during superposition. Furthermore, we show that larger models can solve more ICL tasks in parallel, and better calibrate their output distribution. Our findings offer insights into the latent capabilities of LLMs, further substantiate the perspective of "LLMs as superposition of simulators", and raise questions about the mechanisms enabling simultaneous task execution.

papers.title: Understanding In-Context Learning Beyond Transformers: An Investigation of State Space and Hybrid Architectures
papers.research_question: How does in-context learning (ICL) work internally in state-space and hybrid architectures, and how do these mechanisms compare to transformers across different task types?
papers.core_contribution: This paper extends the analysis of function vectors (FVs) to state-space and hybrid architectures, revealing that while models can exhibit similar ICL performance, their internal mechanisms differ, with FVs being more critical for parametric knowledge retrieval than contextual understanding.
papers.conclusion: The work extends prior analysis of function vectors to diverse architectures and contributes to a more nuanced understanding of FVs across task types, while methodologically highlighting the importance of combining behavioral and mechanistic analyses.
papers.key_findings:
While LLMs of different architectures can behave similarly in task performance, their internal mechanisms can remain different.
Function vectors (FVs) responsible for ICL are primarily located in the self-attention and Mamba layers.
Mamba2 appears to use a different mechanism from FVs to perform ICL.
FVs are more important for ICL involving parametric knowledge retrieval than for contextual knowledge understanding.
In hybrid models, ICL capabilities are primarily contributed by FVs located in self-attention layers, regardless of whether self-attention and SSM layers are stacked in parallel or sequentially.
papers.abstract: We perform in-depth evaluations of in-context learning (ICL) on state-of-the-art transformer, state-space, and hybrid large language models over two categories of knowledge-based ICL tasks. Using a combination of behavioral probing and intervention-based methods, we have discovered that, while LLMs of different architectures can behave similarly in task performance, their internals could remain different. We discover that function vectors (FVs) responsible for ICL are primarily located in the self-attention and Mamba layers, and speculate that Mamba2 uses a different mechanism from FVs to perform ICL. FVs are more important for ICL involving parametric knowledge retrieval, but not for contextual knowledge understanding. Our work contributes to a more nuanced understanding across architectures and task types. Methodologically, our approach also highlights the importance of combining both behavioural and mechanistic analyses to investigate LLM capabilities.

papers.title: Next-token pretraining implies in-context learning
papers.research_question: Does in-context learning emerge as a necessary consequence of next-token pretraining, rather than being an exotic emergent property?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that in-context learning is a mathematically inevitable consequence of optimizing next-token prediction objectives, and provides an information-theoretic framework to predict ICL dynamics for correlated stochastic processes.
papers.conclusion: In-context learning is a natural, predictable outcome of next-token pretraining, grounded in architecture- and modality-independent information-theoretic principles.
papers.key_findings:
In-context learning necessarily arises from next-token pretraining on correlated sequences, rather than being an exotic emergent property.
The reduction of in-context loss (predictive uncertainty) with more context can be precisely predicted using the mixed-state presentation (MSP) of the data-generating process.
Induction heads are a useful mechanism for disambiguating between different ergodic components in non-ergodic training data.
Power-law decay of in-context loss emerges when training on non-ergodic processes or processes with hierarchical correlational structure.
A model's in-context performance on a specific task is mathematically coupled to the entire ensemble of tasks encountered during pretraining.
papers.limitation: The analysis is limited to in-distribution ICL; a full account of out-of-distribution ICL is beyond the current scope.
papers.abstract: We argue that in-context learning (ICL) predictably arises from standard self-supervised next-token pretraining, rather than being an exotic emergent property. This work establishes the foundational principles of this emergence by focusing on in-distribution ICL, demonstrating how models necessarily adapt to context when trained on token sequences, especially from non-ergodic sources. Our information-theoretic framework precisely predicts these in-distribution ICL dynamics (i.e., context-dependent loss reduction). We verify this with experiments using synthetic datasets of differing types of correlational structure, reproducing characteristic phenomena like phase transitions in training loss for induction head formation and power-law scaling of in-context loss. We further show that a model's in-context performance on any task is mathematically coupled to the ensemble of tasks seen in pretraining, offering a fundamental explanation, grounded in architecture- and modality-independent principles, for such inference-time learning.

papers.title: Generating Diverse Translation by Manipulating Multi-Head Attention
papers.research_question: The paper investigates how different attention heads in Transformer's encoder-decoder multi-head attention align to different translation candidates and proposes a method to generate diverse translations by manipulating these heads.
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers that different attention heads in Transformer's encoder-decoder attention align to different translation candidates and proposes a method to generate diverse translations by selectively sampling these heads, improving diversity without severe quality loss.
papers.conclusion: The paper discovers an internal characteristic of Transformer multi-head attention and uses it to generate diverse translations, with applications in back-translation and conversation response generation showing significant improvements.
papers.key_findings:
Different attention heads in the final decoder layer align to different source word translation candidates.
By manipulating these heads, diverse translations can be generated without a severe drop in quality.
The proposed method outperforms previous diversity-enhancing methods in translation tasks.
Using diverse translations for back-translation improves machine translation performance.
The method also enhances diversity in conversation response generation tasks.
papers.abstract: Transformer model has been widely used on machine translation tasks and obtained state-of-the-art results. In this paper, we report an interesting phenomenon in its encoder-decoder multi-head attention: different attention heads of the final decoder layer align to different word translation candidates. We empirically verify this discovery and propose a method to generate diverse translations by manipulating heads. Furthermore, we make use of these diverse translations with the back-translation technique for better data augmentation. Experiment results show that our method generates diverse translations without severe drop in translation quality. Experiments also show that back-translation with these diverse translations could bring significant improvement on performance on translation tasks. An auxiliary experiment of conversation response generation task proves the effect of diversity as well.

papers.title: Provable Low-Frequency Bias of In-Context Learning of Representations
papers.research_question: How does the double convergence process in in-context learning lead to an implicit bias towards smooth (low-frequency) representations?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the double convergence framework to explain the low-frequency bias in in-context learning, providing theoretical explanations for several empirical phenomena.
papers.conclusion: The double convergence phenomenon leads to a low-frequency bias in in-context learning, explaining several observed phenomena and providing a theoretical foundation for future work.
papers.key_findings:
Double convergence (context-wise and layer-wise) leads to an implicit low-frequency bias in hidden representations.
Explains why in-context learning can suppress the original semantic meaning learned during pre-training.
Explains why learned representations form a globally structured but locally distorted geometry.
Explains why the energy of representations decays but does not converge to zero.
Predicts and empirically verifies that in-context learning exhibits intrinsic robustness to high-frequency noise in the input.
papers.limitation: The most detailed results focus on the specific data-generating process (random walk on a graph) from Park et al. (2024), and generalizing to broader data distributions remains an open direction.
future_direction: Generalizing the analysis to broader data distributions.
Analyzing how the structural assumptions on attention maps emerge from pre-training.
papers.abstract: In-context learning (ICL) enables large language models (LLMs) to acquire new behaviors from the input sequence alone without any parameter updates. Recent studies have shown that ICL can surpass the original meaning learned in pretraining stage through internalizing the structure the data-generating process (DGP) of the prompt into the hidden representations. However, the mechanisms by which LLMs achieve this ability is left open. In this paper, we present the first rigorous explanation of such phenomena by introducing a unified framework of double convergence, where hidden representations converge both over context and across layers. This double convergence process leads to an implicit bias towards smooth (low-frequency) representations, which we prove analytically and verify empirically. Our theory explains several open empirical observations, including why learned representations exhibit globally structured but locally distorted geometry, and why their total energy decays without vanishing. Moreover, our theory predicts that ICL has an intrinsic robustness towards high-frequency noise, which we empirically confirm. These results provide new insights into the underlying mechanisms of ICL, and a theoretical foundation to study it that hopefully extends to more general data distributions and settings.

papers.title: Training Dynamics of Contextual N-Grams in Language Models
papers.research_question: How do contextual n-gram circuits form during training? Do they form gradually or in a sudden phase transition?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that contextual n-gram circuits form gradually as second-order circuits, combining pre-existing n-gram and language detection circuits, contrary to the hypothesis that circuits form in sudden phase transitions.
papers.conclusion: The formation of the contextual n-gram circuit is gradual and represents a second-order circuit, adding complexity to the quantization model of neural scaling.
papers.key_findings:
The German context neuron and German trigram prediction are learned early in a phase transition, but the trigram prediction does not depend on the context neuron initially.
The contextual n-gram circuit (where trigram prediction depends on the context neuron) forms gradually later in training.
There is a large cohort of context neurons that form early but are quickly unlearned, and most have low impact on loss.
The direct effect of the context neuron boosts German unigrams, and the indirect effect enables contextual n-grams.
The general phase transition in capabilities coincides with the learning rate warm-up.
papers.limitation: The analysis focused on specifically selected n-grams that strongly rely on the German context neuron, and it is uncertain whether the neuron contributes to other circuits.
future_direction: Fully reverse-engineer the role of context neurons in language models by comprehensively identifying all circuits they are involved in or proving that unigram and n-gram effects are sufficient to explain their effects.
Investigate the emergence and role of the early context neurons that form and are quickly unlearned.
papers.abstract: Prior work has shown the existence of contextual neurons in language models, including a neuron that activates on German text. We show that this neuron exists within a broader contextual n-gram circuit: we find late layer neurons which recognize and continue n-grams common in German text, but which only activate if the German neuron is active. We investigate the formation of this circuit throughout training and find that it is an example of what we call a second-order circuit. In particular, both the constituent n-gram circuits and the German detection circuit which culminates in the German neuron form with independent functions early in training - the German detection circuit partially through modeling German unigram statistics, and the n-grams by boosting appropriate completions. Only after both circuits have already formed do they fit together into a second-order circuit. Contrary to the hypotheses presented in prior work, we find that the contextual n-gram circuit forms gradually rather than in a sudden phase transition. We further present a range of anomalous observations such as a simultaneous phase transition in many tasks coinciding with the learning rate warm-up, and evidence that many context neurons form simultaneously early in training but are later unlearned.

papers.title: The mechanistic basis of data dependence and abrupt learning in an in-context classification task
papers.research_question: What aspects of the training data distribution and architecture favor in-context vs in-weights learning, and what is the mechanistic basis of the abrupt transition observed during in-context learning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that data distributional dependencies for in-context learning are recapitulated in a minimal attention-only network, and that the abrupt transition in ICL is driven by the formation of an induction head, which is explained by a phenomenological model with nested logits.
papers.conclusion: The abrupt transition in ICL is due to the sequential learning of three nested logits in the induction head, and an intrinsic curriculum (slow learning of a simpler strategy) may be necessary to guide the network towards the ICL solution.
papers.key_findings:
Increasing burstiness (B) and number of classes (K) promotes ICL while decreasing IWL.
Within-class variation (ε) promotes ICL and decreases IWL.
A Zipfian rank-frequency distribution (α=1) promotes both ICL and IWL simultaneously.
The network can learn both ICL and IWL solutions simultaneously when trained on a mix of sequences.
The abrupt transition in ICL is driven by the formation of an induction head, preceded by a slow learning phase where the network learns to randomly pick a contextual label.
papers.limitation:
The model is minimal and larger models may use different mechanisms than the ones identified.
The analysis did not use heuristics such as weight tying, which are common in LLMs and might change the learning dynamics.
future_direction: Testing the hypothesis that learning of simpler ICL operations enables the learning of more complex ICL strategies in large language models.
Using methods for mechanistic interpretability to probe these mechanisms in LLMs.
Exploring the role of curricula for accelerating ICL in LLMs.
papers.abstract: Transformer models exhibit in-context learning: the ability to accurately predict the response to a novel query based on illustrative examples in the input sequence. In-context learning contrasts with traditional in-weights learning of query-output relationships. What aspects of the training data distribution and architecture favor in-context vs in-weights learning? Recent work has shown that specific distributional properties inherent in language, such as burstiness, large dictionaries and skewed rank-frequency distributions, control the trade-off or simultaneous appearance of these two forms of learning. We first show that these results are recapitulated in a minimal attention-only network trained on a simplified dataset. In-context learning (ICL) is driven by the abrupt emergence of an induction head, which subsequently competes with in-weights learning. By identifying progress measures that precede in-context learning and targeted experiments, we construct a two-parameter model of an induction head which emulates the full data distributional dependencies displayed by the attention-based network. A phenomenological model of induction head formation traces its abrupt emergence to the sequential learning of three nested logits enabled by an intrinsic curriculum. We propose that the sharp transitions in attention-based networks arise due to a specific chain of multi-layer operations necessary to achieve ICL, which is implemented by nested nonlinearities sequentially learned during training.

papers.title: Unraveling Syntax: How Language Models Learn Context-Free Grammars
papers.research_question: How does language modeling loss decompose with respect to the subgrammar structure of context-free grammars, and do models learn subgrammars in parallel?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that language modeling loss decomposes linearly over the subgrammars of a context-free grammar, and that small transformers learn subgrammars in parallel, unlike children. Subgrammar pretraining can improve performance for tiny models and leads to internal representations that better reflect the grammar's substructure.
papers.conclusion: The work initiates the study of language modeling dynamics with respect to CFG substructure, showing loss decomposes into subgrammar-local contributions and that small transformers learn subgrammars in parallel. Subgrammar pretraining acts as an inductive bias, and depth of recursion remains a challenge.
papers.key_findings:
Language modeling loss (KL divergence) recurses linearly over the top-level subgrammars of a CFG.
Under certain assumptions, parametrized models learn subgrammars in parallel.
Empirically, small transformers learn all subgrammars in parallel, unlike children who master simpler substructures first.
Subgrammar pretraining can improve final performance for tiny models, and leads to internal representations that better align with the grammar's substructure.
Models struggle with deep recursion, even when they achieve low loss on training data.
papers.limitation:
Theoretical results do not fully explain when gradient-based training yields parallel improvement across subgrammars.
Experiments use a small set of synthetic PCFGs and scaled-down transformers, not covering the full diversity of CFGs (e.g., ambiguous grammars).
It is unresolved whether failures at deep recursion reflect representational limits or optimization barriers.
future_direction: Studying when and why models learn subgrammars in parallel.
Understanding why subgrammar pretraining yields more aligned representations and the optimal pretraining duration.
Exploring the effect of ambiguous CFGs and comparing other language classes in the Chomsky hierarchy.
papers.abstract: We introduce a new framework for understanding how language models acquire syntax. While large models achieve impressive results, little is known about their learning dynamics. Our approach starts with the observation that most domains of interest, such as natural language syntax, coding languages, arithmetic problems, are captured by probabilistic context-free grammars (PCFGs). We study the learning dynamics of small models trained on synthetic languages generated from PCFGs, enabling precise control over grammar complexity, recursion depth, and subgrammar structure. We prove several general, recursive formulae for the training loss and Kullback-Leibler divergence over the subgrammar structure of a PCFG. Empirically, we find that unlike children, who first master simple substructures before progressing to more complex constructions, transformers reduce loss across all subgrammars in parallel. We further show that subgrammar pretraining can improve the final loss for smaller models, and that pretrained models develop internal representations more aligned with the grammar's substructure. Finally, we demonstrate that models struggle with deeper recursive structures (a limitation even of large language models), revealing fundamental challenges in how neural networks represent hierarchical syntax. Overall, our work initiates the study of the learning dynamics of transformers on PCFGs as a versatile testbed for probing learning in language models, opening a research direction with many open questions.

papers.title: Towards Opening the Black Box of Neural Machine Translation: Source and Target Interpretations of the Transformer
papers.research_question: How can we measure the contributions of each input token (source sentence and target prefix) to the predictions of encoder-decoder Transformer models in Neural Machine Translation?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes ALTI+, an interpretability method for encoder-decoder Transformers that quantifies the contributions of source and target prefix tokens to model predictions, providing insights into model behavior such as the role of the EOS token and source contribution during hallucinations.
papers.conclusion: ALTI+ provides a method to understand the influences of source and target prefix tokens in NMT models, revealing insights such as the role of the EOS token and source contribution in hallucinations and low-resource scenarios.
papers.key_findings:
The encoder retains a high contribution from the input token at the same position (up to 47% in the multilingual model).
The proposed cross-attention contributions achieve lower Alignment Error Rate (AER) than previous methods.
The EOS token in the source is used to skip source attention and allow information flow from the target prefix.
During hallucinations, the model largely ignores source tokens.
In low-resource translation, the model tends to ignore the source when translating from English to a low-resource language.
papers.limitation: ALTI+ does not consider the softmax layer and thus does not provide explanations for each output class (target vocabulary).
future_direction: Explore and mitigate biases using ALTI+ source input attributions.
papers.abstract: In Neural Machine Translation (NMT), each token prediction is conditioned on the source sentence and the target prefix (what has been previously translated at a decoding step). However, previous work on interpretability in NMT has mainly focused solely on source sentence tokens' attributions. Therefore, we lack a full understanding of the influences of every input token (source sentence and target prefix) in the model predictions. In this work, we propose an interpretability method that tracks input tokens' attributions for both contexts. Our method, which can be extended to any encoder-decoder Transformer-based model, allows us to better comprehend the inner workings of current NMT models. We apply the proposed method to both bilingual and multilingual Transformers and present insights into their behaviour.

papers.title: Label Words as Local Task Vectors in In-Context Learning
papers.research_question: How is task information represented during in-context learning (ICL) in Large Language Models? Specifically, does a single global task vector exist for all tasks, or is information distributed across local task vectors?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that in-context learning (ICL) often relies on distributed local task vectors at the answer positions of each demonstration, rather than a single global task vector, especially for categorization tasks. Patching these local vectors can restore ICL performance.
papers.conclusion: The study reveals a distributed mechanism for ICL using local task vectors that encode abstract task information from each demonstration, providing a more nuanced understanding than the single global task vector hypothesis.
papers.key_findings:
In categorization tasks, task information is distributed across local task vectors at each demonstration's answer position; these vectors do not converge into a single global vector.
In knowledge tasks, local task vectors converge in later layers to form a global task vector, which can be patched for zero-shot performance.
Patching local task vectors from middle layers (6-10) rescues performance in categorization tasks where global vector patching fails.
Saliency and ablation analyses show the answer positions are critical for transmitting task information, with different patterns between knowledge and categorization tasks.
papers.limitation: Neither global nor local task vectors work consistently across all tasks and in all types of LLMs tested.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable abilities, one of the most important being in-context learning (ICL). With ICL, LLMs can derive the underlying rule from a few demonstrations and provide answers that comply with the rule. Previous work hypothesized that the network creates a task vector in specific positions during ICL. The task vector can be computed by averaging across the dataset. It conveys the overall task information and can thus be considered global. Patching the global task vector allows LLMs to achieve zero-shot performance with dummy inputs comparable to few-shot learning. However, we find that such a global task vector does not exist in all tasks, especially in tasks that rely on rules that can only be inferred from multiple demonstrations, such as categorization tasks. Instead, the information provided by each demonstration is first transmitted to its answer position and forms a local task vector associated with the demonstration. In some tasks but not in categorization tasks, all demonstrations' local task vectors converge in later layers, forming the global task vector. We further show that local task vectors encode a high-level abstraction of rules extracted from the demonstrations. Our study provides novel insights into the mechanism underlying ICL in LLMs, demonstrating how ICL may be achieved through an information aggregation mechanism.

papers.title: Identifying and Analyzing Performance-Critical Tokens in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What types of tokens in in-context learning prompts are performance-critical for large language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that in in-context learning, template and stopword tokens are more performance-critical than content tokens, and that content tokens indirectly contribute by aggregating information into performance-critical tokens.
papers.conclusion: Our work sheds light on how LLMs learn to perform tasks from demonstrations and deepens our understanding of the roles different types of tokens play in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Template and stopword tokens are more likely to be performance-critical tokens in ICL.
Content tokens have a negligible direct impact on performance but indirectly contribute through information aggregation.
Lexical meaning, repetition, and structural cues are distinguishing characteristics of performance-critical tokens.
future_direction: Future work to explore how specific token representations can be leveraged for purposes like storing compressed information.
papers.abstract: In-context learning (ICL) has emerged as an effective solution for few-shot learning with large language models (LLMs). However, how LLMs leverage demonstrations to specify a task and learn a corresponding computational function through ICL is underexplored. Drawing from the way humans learn from content-label mappings in demonstrations, we categorize the tokens in an ICL prompt into content, stopword, and template tokens. Our goal is to identify the types of tokens whose representations directly influence LLM's performance, a property we refer to as being performance-critical. By ablating representations from the attention of the test example, we find that the representations of informative content tokens have less influence on performance compared to template and stopword tokens, which contrasts with the human attention to informative words. We give evidence that the representations of performance-critical tokens aggregate information from the content tokens. Moreover, we demonstrate experimentally that lexical meaning, repetition, and structural cues are the main distinguishing characteristics of these tokens. Our work sheds light on how large language models learn to perform tasks from demonstrations and deepens our understanding of the roles different types of tokens play in large language models.

papers.title: Re-examining learning linear functions in context
papers.research_question: How do transformers actually perform in-context learning of linear functions? Do they use linear regression or another mechanism?
papers.core_contribution: Transformers do not use linear regression for in-context learning of linear functions; instead, they exhibit boundary values determined by training data, leading to a trade-off between precision and generalizability.
papers.conclusion: Transformers are theoretically capable of learning linear regression for in-context learning, but in practice they do not; instead, they exhibit boundary values that create a dilemma between accuracy and generalizability.
papers.key_findings:
Attention layers are necessary and sufficient for ICL1 of linear functions; MLP-only models fail.
Models have boundary values (B-, B+) that limit generalization, determined by extreme values seen during training.
There is a trade-off: training on restricted intervals yields high accuracy but poor generalization, while training on larger intervals improves generalization but reduces accuracy.
Models do not perform ICL2 (i.e., they do not infer linear function parameters via linear regression).
Models use the entire sequence for prediction, not just a fixed subsequence.
papers.limitation: The proposed hypothesis about how models learn is not fully verified.
future_direction: Probing what models do at various layers to isolate stages of the learning algorithm.
papers.abstract: In-context learning (ICL) has emerged as a powerful paradigm for easily adapting Large Language Models (LLMs) to various tasks. However, our understanding of how ICL works remains limited. We explore a simple model of ICL in a controlled setup with synthetic training data to investigate ICL of univariate linear functions. We experiment with a range of GPT-2-like transformer models trained from scratch. Our findings challenge the prevailing narrative that transformers adopt algorithmic approaches like linear regression to learn a linear function in-context. These models fail to generalize beyond their training distribution, highlighting fundamental limitations in their capacity to infer abstract task structures. Our experiments lead us to propose a mathematically precise hypothesis of what the model might be learning.

papers.title: What needs to go right for an induction head? A mechanistic study of in-context learning circuits and their formation
papers.research_question: Why is there more than one induction head, and how are they dependent on each other? Why do induction heads appear all of a sudden, and what are the subcircuits that enable them to emerge?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an artificial optogenetics framework for causal manipulation of activations during training and uses it to identify three interacting subcircuits that explain the phase change in induction head formation.
papers.conclusion: The study provides a deeper understanding of induction head formation and phase changes through the identification of subcircuits, and the introduced framework enables causal analysis of training dynamics.
papers.key_findings:
Multiple induction heads form and contribute additively to minimize loss.
Induction heads and previous token heads are wired in a many-to-many fashion.
Three underlying subcircuits (match, copy, and routing) interact to drive the phase change in induction head formation.
The timing of the phase change depends on data properties, which can be understood through the subcircuits.
The network uses additional capacity (multiple heads) for faster training even when not strictly necessary.
papers.abstract: In-context learning is a powerful emergent ability in transformer models. Prior work in mechanistic interpretability has identified a circuit element that may be critical for in-context learning -- the induction head (IH), which performs a match-and-copy operation. During training of large transformers on natural language data, IHs emerge around the same time as a notable phase change in the loss. Despite the robust evidence for IHs and this interesting coincidence with the phase change, relatively little is known about the diversity and emergence dynamics of IHs. Why is there more than one IH, and how are they dependent on each other? Why do IHs appear all of a sudden, and what are the subcircuits that enable them to emerge? We answer these questions by studying IH emergence dynamics in a controlled setting by training on synthetic data. In doing so, we develop and share a novel optogenetics-inspired causal framework for modifying activations throughout training. Using this framework, we delineate the diverse and additive nature of IHs. By clamping subsets of activations throughout training, we then identify three underlying subcircuits that interact to drive IH formation, yielding the phase change. Furthermore, these subcircuits shed light on data-dependent properties of formation, such as phase change timing, already showing the promise of this more in-depth understanding of subcircuits that need to "go right" for an induction head.

papers.title: Unveiling Induction Heads: Provable Training Dynamics and Feature Learning in Transformers
papers.research_question: Does the gradient flow with respect to the cross-entropy loss converge during training? If yes, how does the limiting model perform in-context learning? How do the building blocks of the transformer model contribute to in-context learning?
papers.core_contribution: Proves that gradient flow training of a two-layer transformer on n-gram Markov chains converges to a model that performs a generalized induction head mechanism, elucidating the roles of attention, FFN, and normalization in in-context learning.
papers.conclusion: The paper provides a theoretical understanding of how transformer building blocks collaborate to enable in-context learning via a generalized induction head mechanism.
papers.key_findings:
Gradient flow converges during training of the transformer on in-context learning of n-gram Markov chains.
The limiting model implements a generalized induction head mechanism that selects an information set based on modified chi-square mutual information.
The first attention layer acts as a copier, the feed-forward network with normalization acts as a selector, and the second attention layer acts as a classifier.
Training dynamics occur in three phases: FFN learns the potential parent set, first attention focuses on selected parents, and second attention parameter increases.
The generalized induction head mechanism emerges from the collaboration of all transformer building blocks.
papers.abstract: In-context learning (ICL) is a cornerstone of large language model (LLM) functionality, yet its theoretical foundations remain elusive due to the complexity of transformer architectures. In particular, most existing work only theoretically explains how the attention mechanism facilitates ICL under certain data models. It remains unclear how the other building blocks of the transformer contribute to ICL. To address this question, we study how a two-attention-layer transformer is trained to perform ICL on $n$-gram Markov chain data, where each token in the Markov chain statistically depends on the previous $n$ tokens. We analyze a sophisticated transformer model featuring relative positional embedding, multi-head softmax attention, and a feed-forward layer with normalization. We prove that the gradient flow with respect to a cross-entropy ICL loss converges to a limiting model that performs a generalized version of the induction head mechanism with a learned feature, resulting from the congruous contribution of all the building blocks. In the limiting model, the first attention layer acts as a $\mathit{copier}$, copying past tokens within a given window to each position, and the feed-forward network with normalization acts as a $\mathit{selector}$ that generates a feature vector by only looking at informationally relevant parents from the window. Finally, the second attention layer is a $\mathit{classifier}$ that compares these features with the feature at the output position, and uses the resulting similarity scores to generate the desired output. Our theory is further validated by experiments.

papers.title: Exact Conversion of In-Context Learning to Model Weights in Linearized-Attention Transformers
papers.research_question: How can in-context learning be converted into model weights in linearized-attention transformers to make it permanent and interpretable?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces an exact method to convert in-context learning prompts into model weights for linearized-attention transformers by adding bias terms, and an approximate method for regular transformers.
papers.conclusion: In-context learning can be converted into model weights exactly for linearized attention transformers and approximately for regular transformers, providing a cheap and interpretable way to permanently incorporate context.
papers.key_findings:
Exact conversion of ICL prompts to model weights is possible for linearized-attention transformers through the addition of bias terms.
The conversion algorithm (ICLCA) is computationally inexpensive and only adds about 1% extra parameters.
Experiments on linear attention transformers show the conversion is exact up to numerical rounding errors.
For regular softmax attention transformers (e.g., GPT-2), an approximate conversion method reduces the relative error of logits.
Adding the proposed bias terms can slightly improve training speed on the induction head task.
papers.limitation:
Exact conversion only works for linearized attention transformers; for regular softmax attention, conversion is approximate and depends on kernel approximation quality.
Scalability of the approximate conversion method to larger models depends on the kernel's ability to approximate softmax in pre-trained transformers.
future_direction: Testing the approximate conversion method with more sophisticated kernels.
Exploring how the conversion method works in conjunction with existing fine-tuning methods.
Investigating possible methods to achieve exact conversion for transformers with softmax attention.
papers.abstract: In-Context Learning (ICL) has been a powerful emergent property of large language models that has attracted increasing attention in recent years. In contrast to regular gradient-based learning, ICL is highly interpretable and does not require parameter updates. In this paper, we show that, for linearized transformer networks, ICL can be made explicit and permanent through the inclusion of bias terms. We mathematically demonstrate the equivalence between a model with ICL demonstration prompts and the same model with the additional bias terms. Our algorithm (ICLCA) allows for exact conversion in an inexpensive manner. Existing methods are not exact and require expensive parameter updates. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach through experiments that show the exact incorporation of ICL tokens into a linear transformer. We further suggest how our method can be adapted to achieve cheap approximate conversion of ICL tokens, even in regular transformer networks that are not linearized. Our experiments on GPT-2 show that, even though the conversion is only approximate, the model still gains valuable context from the included bias terms.

papers.title: Can Transformer be Too Compositional? Analysing Idiom Processing in Neural Machine Translation
papers.research_question: How does the Transformer-based neural machine translation model process idioms, and is the non-compositionality of idioms reflected in its mechanics?
papers.core_contribution: Transformer tends to translate idioms too compositionally, and when it produces non-literal translations, the encoder groups idiom parts more strongly as a single unit, with reduced interaction with context and reduced cross-attention on source tokens.
papers.conclusion: Transformer's tendency to process idioms compositionally contributes to literal translations, and techniques that encourage compositionality in NMT may be detrimental for non-compositional phenomena like idioms.
papers.key_findings:
Figurative idioms receive more attention within the PIE in encoder self-attention compared to literal idioms.
Figurative idioms have reduced attention between the PIE and its context.
In cross-attention, figurative idioms lead to reduced attention on source-side PIE tokens and increased attention on the </s> token.
Hidden representations of figurative idioms change more across layers than those of literal idioms.
Intervening with INLP to remove linearly encoded features of figurativeness can change paraphrased translations to word-for-word, indicating a causal link.
papers.limitation:
Heuristic annotation method for translations has imperfect accuracy (75-89% for key categories).
Analysis is limited to seven European languages.
future_direction: Architectural changes to improve grouping of idioms as single units, e.g., training specific attention heads or penalizing overly compositional translations.
Evaluate the effect of compositionality-favouring techniques on non-compositional phenomena like idioms.
papers.abstract: Unlike literal expressions, idioms' meanings do not directly follow from their parts, posing a challenge for neural machine translation (NMT). NMT models are often unable to translate idioms accurately and over-generate compositional, literal translations. In this work, we investigate whether the non-compositionality of idioms is reflected in the mechanics of the dominant NMT model, Transformer, by analysing the hidden states and attention patterns for models with English as source language and one of seven European languages as target language.When Transformer emits a non-literal translation - i.e. identifies the expression as idiomatic - the encoder processes idioms more strongly as single lexical units compared to literal expressions. This manifests in idioms' parts being grouped through attention and in reduced interaction between idioms and their context.In the decoder's cross-attention, figurative inputs result in reduced attention on source-side tokens. These results suggest that Transformer's tendency to process idioms as compositional expressions contributes to literal translations of idioms.

papers.title: The Transient Nature of Emergent In-Context Learning in Transformers
papers.research_question: Is in-context learning (ICL) in transformers a persistent phenomenon, or does it emerge and then disappear (become transient) during training?
papers.core_contribution: In-context learning (ICL) in transformers is often transient: it emerges and then disappears during training, even as training loss decreases, indicating an asymptotic preference for in-weights learning (IWL).
papers.conclusion: In-context learning is often transient, emphasizing the importance of validation metrics, early stopping, or regularization to preserve ICL capabilities during training.
papers.key_findings:
ICL emerges and then disappears (is transient) during training, while IWL accuracy increases.
