ICL transience occurs across a range of model sizes (depth, embedding dimension), dataset sizes (number of classes, exemplars per class), and dataset types (Omniglot images, LLaMa token embeddings).
Data distributional properties, such as a larger number of classes or a Zipfian skew, can postpone the transience of ICL.
L2 regularization can mitigate or eliminate ICL transience, potentially by favoring the lower-norm ICL circuit.
Preliminary evidence suggests ICL transience may be caused by competition between ICL and IWL circuits for resources in the transformer's residual stream.
future_direction: Explore the effect of alternate optimizers or initialization schemes on the transience of ICL.
Connect findings to natural language settings and large-scale language models.
papers.abstract: Transformer neural networks can exhibit a surprising capacity for in-context learning (ICL) despite not being explicitly trained for it. Prior work has provided a deeper understanding of how ICL emerges in transformers, e.g. through the lens of mechanistic interpretability, Bayesian inference, or by examining the distributional properties of training data. However, in each of these cases, ICL is treated largely as a persistent phenomenon; namely, once ICL emerges, it is assumed to persist asymptotically. Here, we show that the emergence of ICL during transformer training is, in fact, often transient. We train transformers on synthetic data designed so that both ICL and in-weights learning (IWL) strategies can lead to correct predictions. We find that ICL first emerges, then disappears and gives way to IWL, all while the training loss decreases, indicating an asymptotic preference for IWL. The transient nature of ICL is observed in transformers across a range of model sizes and datasets, raising the question of how much to "overtrain" transformers when seeking compact, cheaper-to-run models. We find that L2 regularization may offer a path to more persistent ICL that removes the need for early stopping based on ICL-style validation tasks. Finally, we present initial evidence that ICL transience may be caused by competition between ICL and IWL circuits.

papers.title: How Do Vision Transformers Work?
papers.research_question: How do multi-head self-attentions (MSAs) and Vision Transformers (ViTs) work? Specifically, what properties of MSAs improve optimization, how do MSAs differ from convolutional layers (Convs), and how can we harmonize MSAs with Convs?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that MSAs in Vision Transformers act as generalized spatial smoothing, flattening loss landscapes and improving generalization, and are complementary to convolutional layers as low-pass vs. high-pass filters. Based on these insights, the paper proposes AlterNet, a model that alternates Conv and MSA blocks, which outperforms CNNs even on small datasets.
papers.conclusion: MSAs are generalized spatial smoothings that complement Convs, and harmonizing them via an alternating pattern leads to models that outperform CNNs across data regimes.
papers.key_findings:
MSAs improve accuracy and generalization by flattening loss landscapes, primarily due to data specificity rather than long-range dependency.
MSAs are low-pass filters that reduce high-frequency signals and aggregate feature maps, while Convs are high-pass filters that amplify high-frequency signals and diversify feature maps.
ViTs suffer from non-convex losses in small data regimes, which can be alleviated by large datasets or loss landscape smoothing methods.
Multi-stage neural networks behave like series connections of small individual models, and MSAs at the end of a stage play a key role in prediction.
The proposed AlterNet, which alternates Conv and MSA blocks, outperforms CNNs not only on large datasets but also on small datasets.
papers.limitation: The effects of data augmentation on loss landscapes and uncertainty calibration require further investigation.
future_direction: Further investigation into the effects of data augmentation on uncertainty calibration and loss landscapes.
papers.abstract: The success of multi-head self-attentions (MSAs) for computer vision is now indisputable. However, little is known about how MSAs work. We present fundamental explanations to help better understand the nature of MSAs. In particular, we demonstrate the following properties of MSAs and Vision Transformers (ViTs): (1) MSAs improve not only accuracy but also generalization by flattening the loss landscapes. Such improvement is primarily attributable to their data specificity, not long-range dependency. On the other hand, ViTs suffer from non-convex losses. Large datasets and loss landscape smoothing methods alleviate this problem; (2) MSAs and Convs exhibit opposite behaviors. For example, MSAs are low-pass filters, but Convs are high-pass filters. Therefore, MSAs and Convs are complementary; (3) Multi-stage neural networks behave like a series connection of small individual models. In addition, MSAs at the end of a stage play a key role in prediction. Based on these insights, we propose AlterNet, a model in which Conv blocks at the end of a stage are replaced with MSA blocks. AlterNet outperforms CNNs not only in large data regimes but also in small data regimes. The code is available at https://github.com/xxxnell/how-do-vits-work.

papers.title: Dissecting Multimodal In-Context Learning: Modality Asymmetries and Circuit Dynamics in modern Transformers
papers.research_question: What enables transformers to perform multimodal ICL, both in terms of training data statistics and mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: The paper reveals a learning asymmetry in multimodal ICL where the primary modality installs the core ICL circuit, enabling multimodal ICL to emerge with low data complexity in the secondary modality.
papers.conclusion: The paper uncovers a learning asymmetry where the primary modality installs the core ICL circuit, enabling multimodal ICL to emerge with low data complexity in the secondary modality.
papers.key_findings:
RoPE increases the data complexity threshold for ICL emergence.
Multimodal ICL exhibits a learning asymmetry: with high-diversity primary modality, surprisingly low data complexity in the secondary modality suffices.
Scaling up unimodal models favors in-weight memorization over ICL, but scaling improves multimodal ICL.
Multimodal ICL relies on induction-style mechanisms that copy labels from matching in-context exemplars.
Encoders improve multimodal ICL by aligning features and providing discriminative representations.
papers.limitation: Observations on production MLLMs are not intended as a mechanistic explanation due to vastly more complex training regimes, data distributions, and architectural choices that confound clean attribution.
future_direction: Investigate circuit-level robustness.
Explore architectural designs that inherently favor robust reasoning over memorization.
papers.abstract: Transformer-based multimodal large language models often exhibit in-context learning (ICL) abilities. Motivated by this phenomenon, we ask: how do transformers learn to associate information across modalities from in-context examples? We investigate this question through controlled experiments on small transformers trained on synthetic classification tasks, enabling precise manipulation of data statistics and model architecture. We begin by revisiting core principles of unimodal ICL in modern transformers. While several prior findings replicate, we find that Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE) increases the data complexity threshold for ICL. Extending to the multimodal setting reveals a fundamental learning asymmetry: when pretrained on high-diversity data from a primary modality, surprisingly low data complexity in the secondary modality suffices for multimodal ICL to emerge. Mechanistic analysis shows that both settings rely on an induction-style mechanism that copies labels from matching in-context exemplars; multimodal training refines and extends these circuits across modalities. Our findings provide a mechanistic foundation for understanding multimodal ICL in modern transformers and introduce a controlled testbed for future investigation.

papers.title: MALT: Mechanistic Ablation of Lossy Translation in LLMs for a Low-Resource Language: Urdu
papers.research_question: How do LLMs process low-resource languages, and can their performance be improved by mechanistically removing lossy translation features?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs have coherent internal English responses for low-resource language inputs, but lossy translation features in final layers degrade output. Mechanistically ablating these features and using a separate translation model significantly improves performance while preserving cultural nuances.
papers.conclusion: LLMs understand low-resource languages well but generate poorly due to lossy translation features. MALT improves performance by ablating these features and using external translation, preserving cultural context, but further work is needed.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs generate more coherent internal latent responses in English for low-resource language inputs compared to their direct outputs.
Translation features in the final layers of LLMs are lossy for low-resource languages, leading to poor generation quality.
Mechanistically ablating these translation features and using a separate machine translation model significantly improves response quality.
The proposed MALT method preserves cultural nuances of the input language.
Performance improvement varies between models, with Llama-3.2-3b showing greater gains than Gemma-2-2b.
papers.limitation:
Implemented on smaller LLMs; for larger LLMs, translation features may be more distributed, making ablation complex.
Generalization to other low-resource languages is untested.
Errors may stem from ablation of non-translation features or from LLM's poor understanding of input.
Focuses on generating detailed answers, not other formats like conversations or few-shot prompting.
Performance difference between models (e.g., Llama-3.2-3b vs. Gemma-2-2b) requires further investigation.
Cultural nuance preservation is indicated but not quantitatively verified.
future_direction: Refine methods and apply to larger LLMs.
Explore more precise ablation techniques to avoid affecting non-translation features.
Investigate generalization to other low-resource languages.
papers.abstract: LLMs are predominantly trained on English data, which leads to a significant drop in performance on low-resource languages. Understanding how LLMs handle these languages is crucial for improving their effectiveness. This study focuses on Urdu as a use case for exploring the challenges faced by LLMs in processing low-resource languages. LLMs primarily reason in English when prompted in another language, with the final layers acting as translators to convert the English response into the target language. This study finds that even for low-resource languages, the internal latent response of LLMs in English is quite coherent; however, the translation features are lossy and result in poor translations, leading to reduced performance. By mechanistically removing these translation features and using a separate translation model to translate the internal latent response of LLM, the performance of LLMs improves significantly while also preserving the cultural nuances of the input in low-resource languages.

papers.title: Toward Understanding In-context vs. In-weight Learning
papers.research_question: How do distributional properties of training data affect the emergence and transience of in-context learning (ICL) versus in-weight learning (IWL) in transformer models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a theoretical and experimental demonstration that in-context learning emerges when training data contains many rare classes (in-context data) and diminishes when sufficient in-weight data is available, explaining the transience of ICL.
papers.conclusion: Simple distributional properties of training data can explain the emergence and eventual disappearance of in-context learning, with ICL and IWL coexisting or dominating depending on the data characteristics.
papers.key_findings:
ICL emerges when there are many rare classes in the training data, as IWL performs poorly on such classes due to insufficient samples.
ICL can become transient when more data is seen, as IWL improves with more samples and eventually outperforms ICL.
The balance between ICL and IWL depends on distributional properties such as the proportion of common vs. rare classes and the relevance of context.
Experiments on synthetic and Omniglot data confirm the theoretical predictions, showing aligned behavior between the simplified model and full transformers.
Fine-tuning a large language model (Gemini Nano) to memorize specific facts reduces its ICL ability, demonstrating that IWL can override ICL.
papers.limitation: The theory does not fully explain the case where ICL and IWL can achieve the same asymptotic performance, leaving open questions about transience in that scenario.
future_direction: Further investigation of the transience of ICL when ICL and IWL have equal performance.
papers.abstract: It has recently been demonstrated empirically that in-context learning emerges in transformers when certain distributional properties are present in the training data, but this ability can also diminish upon further training. We provide a new theoretical understanding of these phenomena by identifying simplified distributional properties that give rise to the emergence and eventual disappearance of in-context learning. We do so by first analyzing a simplified model that uses a gating mechanism to choose between an in-weight and an in-context predictor. Through a combination of a generalization error and regret analysis we identify conditions where in-context and in-weight learning emerge. These theoretical findings are then corroborated experimentally by comparing the behaviour of a full transformer on the simplified distributions to that of the stylized model, demonstrating aligned results. We then extend the study to a full large language model, showing how fine-tuning on various collections of natural language prompts can elicit similar in-context and in-weight learning behaviour.

papers.title: Locating and Editing Factual Associations in GPT
papers.research_question: How are factual associations stored and recalled in autoregressive transformer language models, and can they be directly edited?
papers.core_contribution: Factual associations in GPT are stored in mid-layer feed-forward modules and can be directly edited using a rank-one update method (ROME), which achieves strong generalization and specificity.
papers.conclusion: Factual associations in autoregressive transformers are stored in mid-layer MLP modules and can be directly edited via localized weight updates, with ROME providing an effective method for such edits.
papers.key_findings:
Causal tracing reveals that mid-layer MLP modules at the last subject token are decisive for factual predictions.
The Rank-One Model Editing (ROME) method can effectively edit factual associations by updating a single MLP layer with a rank-one weight update.
ROME achieves strong generalization and specificity on counterfactual edits, outperforming previous fine-tuning and hypernetwork-based methods.
The early site (mid-layer MLP) and late site (late-layer attention) play different roles: MLP stores the association, and attention copies it to the output.
The paper introduces a new dataset, COUNTERFACT, for evaluating counterfactual model edits.
papers.limitation: Human evaluation reveals a reduction in fluency of generated text under ROME, which the automatic entropy measure does not capture.
papers.abstract: We analyze the storage and recall of factual associations in autoregressive transformer language models, finding evidence that these associations correspond to localized, directly-editable computations. We first develop a causal intervention for identifying neuron activations that are decisive in a model's factual predictions. This reveals a distinct set of steps in middle-layer feed-forward modules that mediate factual predictions while processing subject tokens. To test our hypothesis that these computations correspond to factual association recall, we modify feed-forward weights to update specific factual associations using Rank-One Model Editing (ROME). We find that ROME is effective on a standard zero-shot relation extraction (zsRE) model-editing task, comparable to existing methods. To perform a more sensitive evaluation, we also evaluate ROME on a new dataset of counterfactual assertions, on which it simultaneously maintains both specificity and generalization, whereas other methods sacrifice one or another. Our results confirm an important role for mid-layer feed-forward modules in storing factual associations and suggest that direct manipulation of computational mechanisms may be a feasible approach for model editing. The code, dataset, visualizations, and an interactive demo notebook are available at https://rome.baulab.info/

papers.title: Interpreting and improving natural-language processing (in machines) with natural language-processing (in the brain)
papers.research_question: How can brain activity recordings be used to interpret neural network representations, and can aligning models with brain activity improve their language understanding?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a method to interpret neural network representations by aligning them with brain activity recordings, and shows that increasing brain-alignment in BERT improves its performance on syntactic tasks.
papers.conclusion: Aligning NLP models with brain activity can provide insights into their representations and lead to improved language understanding, as demonstrated by improved syntactic performance of brain-altered BERT.
papers.key_findings:
Middle layers of transformers are better at predicting brain activity for longer contexts.
Transformer-XL's performance does not degrade with longer context, unlike other models.
Uniform attention in shallow layers of BERT improves brain activity prediction for contexts up to 25 words.
Altering BERT to have uniform attention in shallow layers improves its performance on syntactic tasks.
Different models (ELMo, USE, BERT, Transformer-XL) encode context information differently.
papers.limitation:
Reverse inference in brain imaging can lead to erroneous conclusions because a brain region can be involved in more than one task.
Direct comparison of performance between different networks is misleading because information is likely organized differently across networks.
papers.abstract: Neural networks models for NLP are typically implemented without the explicit encoding of language rules and yet they are able to break one performance record after another. This has generated a lot of research interest in interpreting the representations learned by these networks. We propose here a novel interpretation approach that relies on the only processing system we have that does understand language: the human brain. We use brain imaging recordings of subjects reading complex natural text to interpret word and sequence embeddings from 4 recent NLP models - ELMo, USE, BERT and Transformer-XL. We study how their representations differ across layer depth, context length, and attention type. Our results reveal differences in the context-related representations across these models. Further, in the transformer models, we find an interaction between layer depth and context length, and between layer depth and attention type. We finally hypothesize that altering BERT to better align with brain recordings would enable it to also better understand language. Probing the altered BERT using syntactic NLP tasks reveals that the model with increased brain-alignment outperforms the original model. Cognitive neuroscientists have already begun using NLP networks to study the brain, and this work closes the loop to allow the interaction between NLP and cognitive neuroscience to be a true cross-pollination.

papers.title: Learning vs Retrieval: The Role of In-Context Examples in Regression with Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What is the underlying mechanism of in-context learning (ICL) in Large Language Models? Specifically, to what extent do LLMs retrieve internal knowledge versus learn from in-context examples during regression tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a new hypothesis and evaluation framework for in-context learning (ICL), arguing that ICL in LLMs is not purely learning or knowledge retrieval but operates on a spectrum between the two, which can be controlled via prompt engineering. Demonstrates this through extensive regression experiments on realistic datasets.
papers.conclusion: In-context learning in LLMs is best understood as a spectrum between learning from examples and retrieving internal knowledge. The balance can be controlled through prompt engineering, such as revealing feature names, to optimize performance for regression tasks.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs can effectively perform regression on realistic datasets using in-context examples.
The ICL mechanism is a combination of learning from examples and retrieving internal knowledge; this balance shifts based on factors like the number of examples and the presence of feature names.
Providing feature names (enabling knowledge retrieval) improves performance, especially with few in-context examples, making LLMs more data-efficient than classical ML models in low-data regimes.
Randomizing the ground truth values in examples significantly degrades performance, demonstrating that LLMs do learn from the output labels in the examples.
Adding more features generally improves performance, primarily enhancing knowledge retrieval rather than learning when many examples are provided.
papers.limitation:
Scope limited to regression tasks and three specific datasets.
Treats LLMs as black boxes; underlying neural mechanisms remain opaque.
Token limits of some LLMs constrained testing beyond 100 in-context examples and three features in certain combinations.
Challenging to distinguish data contamination from approximate knowledge retrieval.
future_direction: Investigate more regression (or classification) datasets with different characteristics to elaborate on the findings.
Integrate the black-box evaluation approach with interpretability techniques for a deeper understanding of ICL mechanisms.
Use datasets from regions beyond the primary training domain of LLMs to mitigate data contamination concerns.
papers.abstract: Generative Large Language Models (LLMs) are capable of being in-context learners. However, the underlying mechanism of in-context learning (ICL) is still a major research question, and experimental research results about how models exploit ICL are not always consistent. In this work, we propose a framework for evaluating in-context learning mechanisms, which we claim are a combination of retrieving internal knowledge and learning from in-context examples by focusing on regression tasks. First, we show that LLMs can solve real-world regression problems and then design experiments to measure the extent to which the LLM retrieves its internal knowledge versus learning from in-context examples. We argue that this process lies on a spectrum between these two extremes. We provide an in-depth analysis of the degrees to which these mechanisms are triggered depending on various factors, such as prior knowledge about the tasks and the type and richness of the information provided by the in-context examples. We employ three LLMs and utilize multiple datasets to corroborate the robustness of our findings. Our results shed light on how to engineer prompts to leverage meta-learning from in-context examples and foster knowledge retrieval depending on the problem being addressed.

papers.title: On the Relationship Between the Choice of Representation and In-Context Learning
papers.research_question: How do representation (choice of label sets) and learning (from demonstrations) interact in in-context learning? The paper hypothesizes that they are independent, with representation setting the baseline accuracy and learning improving on top of that baseline.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that in-context learning performance is influenced independently by representation (label sets) and learning (number of demonstrations). Representation sets the baseline accuracy, and learning improves on top of it, with the relative quality of label sets remaining consistent across different numbers of demonstrations.
papers.conclusion: The study reveals that representation and learning are largely independent in ICL, with representation setting the baseline accuracy and learning improving on top, emphasizing the importance of label set choice in ICL studies.
papers.key_findings:
Learning (improvement with more demonstrations) happens regardless of label set quality, though its efficiency depends on model size and label set quality.
The ranking of label sets by accuracy remains constant across different numbers of demonstrations.
Representation limits the range of accuracies attainable; low zero-shot accuracy label sets are hard to overcome even with many demonstrations.
Model size influences learning rate: larger models learn faster (steeper curves).
For a given label set, the N-shot accuracy generally increases with N, but the slope varies.
future_direction: Extend the study to more complex reasoning tasks.
Investigate how changes in problem representation affect reasoning failures.
papers.abstract: In-context learning (ICL) is the ability of a large language model (LLM) to learn a new task from a few demonstrations presented as part of the context. Past studies have attributed a large portion of the success of ICL to the way these in-context demonstrations are represented, particularly to how labels are represented in classification tasks. On the other hand, observations of the learning capacity of ICL (i.e., the extent to which more in-context demonstrations can lead to higher performance) have been mixed, and ICL is often thought to occur only under specific conditions. The interaction between these two aspects in ICL, representation and learning, has not been studied in depth until now. We hypothesize that they are largely independent of one another, such that the representation of demonstrations determines the baseline accuracy of ICL, while learning from additional demonstrations improves only on top of this baseline. We validate this hypothesis by developing an optimization algorithm that can enumerate a spectrum of possible label sets (representations) varying in semantic relevance. We then perform ICL with varying numbers of in-context demonstrations for each of these label sets. We observed that learning happens regardless of the quality of the label set itself, although its efficiency, measured by the slope of improvement over in-context demonstrations, is conditioned on both the label set quality and the parameter count of the underlying language model. Despite the emergence of learning, the relative quality (accuracy) of the choice of a label set (representation) is largely maintained throughout learning, confirming our hypothesis and implying their orthogonality. Our work reveals a previously underexplored aspect of ICL: the independent effects of learning from demonstrations and their representations on ICL performance.

papers.title: Towards Understanding How Transformers Learn In-context Through a Representation Learning Lens
papers.research_question: How does in-context learning (ICL) in Transformers work? Can ICL be related to gradient descent under the softmax attention setting without specific constructions for model weights and input tokens?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that the ICL inference process of a softmax attention layer is equivalent to gradient descent on a dual model, provides a representation learning interpretation, derives a generalization bound, and proposes attention modifications inspired by contrastive learning.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that ICL can be understood as gradient descent on a dual model from a representation learning perspective, and that attention modifications inspired by this view show promise in enhancing model performance.
papers.key_findings:
The ICL inference of a softmax attention layer is equivalent to one step of gradient descent on a dual model with a loss function that maximizes similarity between value-projected and key-projected tokens.
The dual model's training resembles a self-supervised representation learning process, analogous to contrastive learning without negative samples.
A generalization error bound for ICL is derived, showing the error decreases with the number of demonstration tokens.
The equivalence extends to a full Transformer layer (with FFN) and multiple attention layers.
Attention modifications inspired by representation learning (regularization, data augmentation, negative samples) can improve model performance on synthetic and GLUE tasks.
papers.limitation:
The negative sample selection method is too coarse and not always effective.
The attention modifications are tested on limited tasks and may not generalize.
future_direction: Develop more task-specific augmentation strategies for attention.
Design more effective methods for constructing negative samples in the attention mechanism.
Apply the representation learning lens to other model components and settings.
papers.abstract: Pre-trained large language models based on Transformers have demonstrated remarkable in-context learning (ICL) abilities. With just a few demonstration examples, the models can implement new tasks without any parameter updates. However, it is still an open question to understand the mechanism of ICL. In this paper, we attempt to explore the ICL process in Transformers through a lens of representation learning. Initially, leveraging kernel methods, we figure out a dual model for one softmax attention layer. The ICL inference process of the attention layer aligns with the training procedure of its dual model, generating token representation predictions that are equivalent to the dual model's test outputs. We delve into the training process of this dual model from a representation learning standpoint and further derive a generalization error bound related to the quantity of demonstration tokens. Subsequently, we extend our theoretical conclusions to more complicated scenarios, including one Transformer layer and multiple attention layers. Furthermore, drawing inspiration from existing representation learning methods especially contrastive learning, we propose potential modifications for the attention layer. Finally, experiments are designed to support our findings.

papers.title: Identifying and Controlling Important Neurons in Neural Machine\n Translation
papers.research_question: How important are individual neurons for obtaining high-quality translations? Do individual neurons in NMT models contain interpretable linguistic information? Can we control MT output by intervening in the representation at the individual neuron level?
papers.core_contribution: The paper develops unsupervised methods (based on correlations between models) for discovering important neurons in Neural Machine Translation models, shows these neurons impact translation quality and capture linguistic phenomena, and demonstrates how to control translations by modifying their activations.
papers.conclusion: The work indicates that not all information is distributed in NMT models, and that many human-interpretable grammatical and structural properties are captured by individual neurons. Moreover, modifying the activations of individual neurons allows controlling the translation output according to specified linguistic properties.
papers.key_findings:
Unsupervised correlation methods (MaxCorr, MinCorr, LinReg, SVCCA) can rank neurons by importance, with top-ranked neurons having a larger impact on translation quality when erased.
Many top-ranked neurons capture interpretable linguistic properties such as position in sentence, parentheses, tense, number, gender, and noun phrase segmentation.
Modifying the activations of individual neurons (e.g., tense neurons) allows for controlling translation output (e.g., changing verb tense) with varying degrees of success.
Different ranking methods highlight different types of information: MaxCorr and MinCorr tend to find position information, while LinReg and SVCCA find information distributed across tokens.
The work indicates that not all linguistic information in NMT models is fully distributed; some properties are captured by individual neurons.
future_direction: Extend the analysis to other NMT components (e.g., the decoder) and architectures (e.g., Transformer, convolutional seq2seq).
Develop more sophisticated ways to control translation output, for example by modifying representations in variational NMT architectures.
Apply the methods to other tasks beyond machine translation.
papers.abstract:
Neural machine translation (NMT) models learn representations containing
substantial linguistic information. However, it is not clear if such
information is fully distributed or if some of it can be attributed to
individual neurons. We develop unsupervised methods for discovering important
neurons in NMT models. Our methods rely on the intuition that different models
learn similar properties, and do not require any costly external supervision.
We show experimentally that translation quality depends on the discovered
neurons, and find that many of them capture common linguistic phenomena.
Finally, we show how to control NMT translations in predictable ways, by
modifying activations of individual neurons.

papers.title: What Can Transformers Learn In-Context? A Case Study of Simple Function Classes
papers.research_question: Can we train a model to in-context learn a function class? What is the relationship between tasks on which in-context learning succeeds and the training data?
papers.core_contribution: Transformers can be trained from scratch to perform in-context learning of simple function classes (e.g., linear functions) with performance comparable to optimal estimators, and this ability generalizes under distribution shifts and extends to more complex function classes.
papers.conclusion: Transformers can encode complex learning algorithms for in-context learning of various function classes, generalizing under distribution shifts, and this work lays groundwork for future research on in-context learning.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers can be trained to in-context learn linear functions with error comparable to the optimal least squares estimator.
The trained model generalizes to out-of-distribution prompts, including shifts in input distributions, label noise, and mismatches between in-context examples and query inputs.
Transformers can in-context learn more complex function classes (sparse linear functions, two-layer neural networks, decision trees) with performance matching or exceeding specialized algorithms like Lasso or gradient descent.
Model capacity and problem dimensionality affect in-context learning performance; larger models handle higher dimensions and distribution shifts better.
Curriculum learning drastically speeds up training without significantly affecting final performance.
papers.limitation:
Understanding the implications of these results for large language models requires further investigation.
Model performance degrades under some distribution shifts, e.g., with skewed covariance or extreme scaling of prompt inputs.
future_direction: Investigating the complexity of in-context learning in terms of function class, model capacity, and training data.
Understanding why curriculum learning speeds up training and whether similar speedups are possible for large language models.
Comparing inductive biases of different model families (e.g., Transformers vs. LSTMs) for in-context learning.
papers.abstract: In-context learning refers to the ability of a model to condition on a prompt sequence consisting of in-context examples (input-output pairs corresponding to some task) along with a new query input, and generate the corresponding output. Crucially, in-context learning happens only at inference time without any parameter updates to the model. While large language models such as GPT-3 exhibit some ability to perform in-context learning, it is unclear what the relationship is between tasks on which this succeeds and what is present in the training data. To make progress towards understanding in-context learning, we consider the well-defined problem of training a model to in-context learn a function class (e.g., linear functions): that is, given data derived from some functions in the class, can we train a model to in-context learn "most" functions from this class? We show empirically that standard Transformers can be trained from scratch to perform in-context learning of linear functions -- that is, the trained model is able to learn unseen linear functions from in-context examples with performance comparable to the optimal least squares estimator. In fact, in-context learning is possible even under two forms of distribution shift: (i) between the training data of the model and inference-time prompts, and (ii) between the in-context examples and the query input during inference. We also show that we can train Transformers to in-context learn more complex function classes -- namely sparse linear functions, two-layer neural networks, and decision trees -- with performance that matches or exceeds task-specific learning algorithms. Our code and models are available at https://github.com/dtsip/in-context-learning .

papers.title: Understanding In-Context Learning in Transformers and LLMs by Learning to Learn Discrete Functions
papers.research_question: What are the limits of in-context learning in Transformers, is attention necessary, can Transformers exploit teaching sequences for efficiency, and to what extent can LLMs implement learning algorithms from in-context examples?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that Transformers can implement near-optimal learning algorithms for simple Boolean functions, struggle with complex ones like parities, and can adaptively use teaching sequences for sample efficiency. Additionally, pretrained LLMs demonstrate non-trivial in-context learning abilities on discrete tasks.
papers.conclusion: The study advances understanding of in-context learning in Transformers and LLMs, showing their capabilities and limitations on discrete function learning, and highlights the potential for adaptive algorithm selection.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers achieve near-perfect accuracy on simple Boolean functions like conjunctions and disjunctions.
Transformers fail to learn parity functions effectively, performing no better than random guessing.
Attention-free models such as Hyena perform similarly to Transformers on most tasks, with minor gaps on some.
Transformers can learn from teaching sequences and implement sample-efficient algorithms, adapting based on input.
Pretrained LLMs like GPT-4 and LLaMA-2 can compete with nearest-neighbor baselines on Boolean function tasks not in their training set.
papers.limitation: Transformers fail to learn parity functions effectively, performing no better than random guessing.
papers.abstract: In order to understand the in-context learning phenomenon, recent works have adopted a stylized experimental framework and demonstrated that Transformers can learn gradient-based learning algorithms for various classes of real-valued functions. However, the limitations of Transformers in implementing learning algorithms, and their ability to learn other forms of algorithms are not well understood. Additionally, the degree to which these capabilities are confined to attention-based models is unclear. Furthermore, it remains to be seen whether the insights derived from these stylized settings can be extrapolated to pretrained Large Language Models (LLMs). In this work, we take a step towards answering these questions by demonstrating the following: (a) On a test-bed with a variety of Boolean function classes, we find that Transformers can nearly match the optimal learning algorithm for 'simpler' tasks, while their performance deteriorates on more 'complex' tasks. Additionally, we find that certain attention-free models perform (almost) identically to Transformers on a range of tasks. (b) When provided a teaching sequence, i.e. a set of examples that uniquely identifies a function in a class, we show that Transformers learn more sample-efficiently. Interestingly, our results show that Transformers can learn to implement two distinct algorithms to solve a single task, and can adaptively select the more sample-efficient algorithm depending on the sequence of in-context examples. (c) Lastly, we show that extant LLMs, e.g. LLaMA-2, GPT-4, can compete with nearest-neighbor baselines on prediction tasks that are guaranteed to not be in their training set.

papers.title: Do Vision Transformers See Like Convolutional Neural Networks?
papers.research_question: How are Vision Transformers solving image tasks? Are they acting like convolutional networks, or learning entirely different visual representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds key representational differences between Vision Transformers (ViTs) and Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), showing ViTs have more uniform layer representations, incorporate global information earlier via self-attention, and have stronger skip connections that propagate features differently.
papers.conclusion: ViTs and CNNs have clear differences in features and internal structure, with ViTs using global features early and strong skip connections, while local information aggregation is learned from scratch at scale. ViTs show strong spatial localization, promising for future uses like object detection.
papers.key_findings:
ViTs have a more uniform internal representation structure with greater similarity between lower and higher layers compared to the staged similarity in ResNets.
ViTs incorporate global information in lower layers through self-attention, while CNNs are restricted to local receptive fields; this leads to quantitatively different features.
Skip connections in ViTs are more influential than in ResNets, with a phase transition: early layers strongly propagate the CLS token, while later layers propagate spatial token representations.
ViTs preserve input spatial information more faithfully than ResNets in higher layers, especially when trained with a CLS token rather than global average pooling.
Large-scale pretraining data is crucial for ViTs to learn to attend locally in early layers and to develop high-quality intermediate representations for transfer learning.
papers.limitation: The study uses CKA, which summarizes measurements into a single scalar; while complemented with interventional tests and linear probes, more fine-grained methods may reveal additional insights.
papers.abstract: Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have so far been the de-facto model for visual data. Recent work has shown that (Vision) Transformer models (ViT) can achieve comparable or even superior performance on image classification tasks. This raises a central question: how are Vision Transformers solving these tasks? Are they acting like convolutional networks, or learning entirely different visual representations? Analyzing the internal representation structure of ViTs and CNNs on image classification benchmarks, we find striking differences between the two architectures, such as ViT having more uniform representations across all layers. We explore how these differences arise, finding crucial roles played by self-attention, which enables early aggregation of global information, and ViT residual connections, which strongly propagate features from lower to higher layers. We study the ramifications for spatial localization, demonstrating ViTs successfully preserve input spatial information, with noticeable effects from different classification methods. Finally, we study the effect of (pretraining) dataset scale on intermediate features and transfer learning, and conclude with a discussion on connections to new architectures such as the MLP-Mixer.

papers.title: Theoretical Understanding of In-Context Learning in Shallow Transformers with Unstructured Data
papers.research_question: How can transformers learn from unstructured data (where input and output are in separate tokens) in in-context learning, and what roles do components like attention layers, attention mask, and positional encoding play?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that a two-layer transformer with a look-ahead attention mask is necessary to learn from unstructured data in ICL, and that positional encoding improves performance by matching input and output tokens.
papers.conclusion: Two attention layers and an attention mask are crucial for learning from unstructured data in ICL, and positional encoding further enhances performance by facilitating token matching.
papers.key_findings:
A one-layer transformer fails to learn from unstructured data in ICL.
A two-layer transformer with a look-ahead attention mask can successfully learn from unstructured data.
Positional encoding helps match input and output tokens, improving ICL performance.
A larger embedding dimension allows the model to handle more in-context examples.
papers.limitation: The paper only considers a simple transformer architecture, which may not capture the full characteristics of transformers used in real practice.
future_direction: Analyzing the effect of using softmax attention in the second layer.
Studying the effect of having more than two attention layers.
Investigating the effect of positional encoding on training dynamics and generalization.
Extending the analysis to chain-of-thought.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are powerful models that can learn concepts at the inference stage via in-context learning (ICL). While theoretical studies, e.g., \cite{zhang2023trained}, attempt to explain the mechanism of ICL, they assume the input $x_i$ and the output $y_i$ of each demonstration example are in the same token (i.e., structured data). However, in real practice, the examples are usually text input, and all words, regardless of their logic relationship, are stored in different tokens (i.e., unstructured data \cite{wibisono2023role}). To understand how LLMs learn from the unstructured data in ICL, this paper studies the role of each component in the transformer architecture and provides a theoretical understanding to explain the success of the architecture. In particular, we consider a simple transformer with one/two attention layers and linear regression tasks for the ICL prediction. We observe that (1) a transformer with two layers of (self-)attentions with a look-ahead attention mask can learn from the prompt in the unstructured data, and (2) positional encoding can match the $x_i$ and $y_i$ tokens to achieve a better ICL performance.

papers.title: Analyzing Multi-Head Self-Attention: Specialized Heads Do the Heavy\n Lifting, the Rest Can Be Pruned
papers.research_question: What is the contribution of individual attention heads to translation performance? Do they play consistent and interpretable roles? Can the number of heads be significantly reduced without serious performance loss?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that only a subset of attention heads are important for translation, with interpretable functions, and introduces a pruning method that can remove the majority of heads without significant performance loss.
papers.conclusion: Specialized attention heads are most important for translation and can be identified, while many heads are redundant and can be pruned without serious performance loss.
papers.key_findings:
Only a small subset of attention heads are important for translation.
Important heads have specialized and interpretable functions, such as attending to adjacent tokens, specific syntactic relations, and rare words.
The proposed pruning method can remove the vast majority of heads (e.g., 38 out of 48 encoder heads) with only a small drop in BLEU (0.15).
Encoder self-attention heads are pruned first, while decoder-encoder attention heads are the most important.
Lower decoder layers retain self-attention heads for language modeling, while higher decoder layers retain decoder-encoder attention heads for conditioning on the source sentence.
papers.limitation: The impact of target language morphology on the accuracy of syntactic attention heads is not fully understood.
future_direction: Investigate how the pruning method compares to alternative methods of model compression in neural machine translation.
papers.abstract:
Multi-head self-attention is a key component of the Transformer, a
state-of-the-art architecture for neural machine translation. In this work we
evaluate the contribution made by individual attention heads in the encoder to
the overall performance of the model and analyze the roles played by them. We
find that the most important and confident heads play consistent and often
linguistically-interpretable roles. When pruning heads using a method based on
stochastic gates and a differentiable relaxation of the L0 penalty, we observe
that specialized heads are last to be pruned. Our novel pruning method removes
the vast majority of heads without seriously affecting performance. For
example, on the English-Russian WMT dataset, pruning 38 out of 48 encoder heads
results in a drop of only 0.15 BLEU.

papers.title: Exploring the Translation Mechanism of Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What are the crucial components and their behavioral patterns in LLM translation, and can fine-tuning these components enhance translation capability?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a framework using subspace-intervened path patching to identify sparse, specialized components crucial for LLM translation, and shows that fine-tuning these components improves translation while preserving general capabilities.
papers.conclusion: The translation mechanism in LLMs is driven by a sparse set of specialized components, and targeted intervention on these components can enhance translation performance without harming general capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Only a sparse subset of heads (less than 5%) are crucial for LLMs’ translation.
Crucial heads exhibit specialized functions (source, indicator, positional) and MLPs integrate their features into English-centric latent representations.
Fine-tuning merely 64 heads achieves performance parity with full-parameter fine-tuning.
These crucial components generalize to sentence-level translation and other tasks (mathematical reasoning).
The translation mechanism is largely established during pre-training, not fine-tuning.
papers.limitation: The analysis is primarily conducted on word-level translation, which may not fully capture the complexities of sentence-level translation.
papers.abstract: While large language models (LLMs) demonstrate remarkable success in multilingual translation, their internal core translation mechanisms, even at the fundamental word level, remain insufficiently understood. To address this critical gap, this work introduces a systematic framework for interpreting the mechanism behind LLM translation from the perspective of computational components. This paper first proposes subspace-intervened path patching for precise, fine-grained causal analysis, enabling the detection of components crucial to translation tasks and subsequently characterizing their behavioral patterns in human-interpretable terms. Comprehensive experiments reveal that translation is predominantly driven by a sparse subset of components: specialized attention heads serve critical roles in extracting source language, translation indicators, and positional features, which are then integrated and processed by specific multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) into intermediary English-centric latent representations before ultimately yielding the final translation. The significance of these findings is underscored by the empirical demonstration that targeted fine-tuning a minimal parameter subset ($<5\%$) enhances translation performance while preserving general capabilities. This result further indicates that these crucial components generalize effectively to sentence-level translation and are instrumental in elucidating more intricate translation tasks.

papers.title: Sudden Drops in the Loss: Syntax Acquisition, Phase Transitions, and Simplicity Bias in MLMs
papers.research_question: How does syntactic attention structure (SAS) emerge during training of masked language models, and what is its causal role in the development of grammatical capabilities?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that syntactic attention structure (SAS) emerges abruptly during training and is necessary for grammatical capabilities; briefly suppressing SAS early in training can improve model quality by allowing an alternative strategy to emerge.
papers.conclusion: Developmental analysis of training dynamics is crucial for understanding model behavior, and SAS represents a simplicity bias that can be manipulated to improve training.
papers.key_findings:
SAS emerges abruptly during training in a phase transition called the structure onset.
The structure onset precedes and is necessary for the capabilities onset, which marks improvements in grammatical capabilities.
Suppressing SAS throughout training prevents the development of grammatical capabilities.
Briefly suppressing SAS early in training improves model quality and accelerates convergence.
There exists an alternative strategy that competes with SAS, and suppressing SAS allows this alternative strategy to emerge earlier.
papers.abstract: Most interpretability research in NLP focuses on understanding the behavior and features of a fully trained model. However, certain insights into model behavior may only be accessible by observing the trajectory of the training process. We present a case study of syntax acquisition in masked language models (MLMs) that demonstrates how analyzing the evolution of interpretable artifacts throughout training deepens our understanding of emergent behavior. In particular, we study Syntactic Attention Structure (SAS), a naturally emerging property of MLMs wherein specific Transformer heads tend to focus on specific syntactic relations. We identify a brief window in pretraining when models abruptly acquire SAS, concurrent with a steep drop in loss. This breakthrough precipitates the subsequent acquisition of linguistic capabilities. We then examine the causal role of SAS by manipulating SAS during training, and demonstrate that SAS is necessary for the development of grammatical capabilities. We further find that SAS competes with other beneficial traits during training, and that briefly suppressing SAS improves model quality. These findings offer an interpretation of a real-world example of both simplicity bias and breakthrough training dynamics.

papers.title: Emergent Linear Representations in World Models of Self-Supervised Sequence Models
papers.research_question: What is the nature of feature representations in sequence models? Specifically, are world models linearly encoded in the activation space?
papers.core_contribution: The board state in OthelloGPT is linearly encoded relative to the current player (MINE vs. YOURS), enabling control of the model's behavior via simple vector arithmetic.
papers.conclusion: The emergent world model in OthelloGPT is linearly represented, enabling interpretability and control via vector arithmetic, and revealing multiple circuits and iterative refinement across layers.
papers.key_findings:
OthelloGPT linearly encodes the board state relative to the current player (MINE/YOURS) rather than absolute colors, achieving high accuracy with linear probes.
Simple vector addition of linear directions (MINE, YOURS, EMPTY) to the residual stream can causally alter the model's believed board state and move predictions.
The model also linearly encodes which tiles are flipped at each timestep, as shown by high F1 scores with linear probes.
Evidence suggests multiple circuits exist: in end games, legal moves are sometimes computed before the full board state is accurately represented.
The model iteratively refines board state and move predictions across layers, with accuracy improving layer by layer.
papers.limitation:
Probing requires knowing which features to look for, and human preconceptions may lead to incorrect interpretations.
The model's board state accuracy drops in end games, and it may use alternative circuits, indicating incomplete understanding.
future_direction: Investigate why linear feature representations emerge and what linear representations exist in large language models.
papers.abstract: How do sequence models represent their decision-making process? Prior work suggests that Othello-playing neural network learned nonlinear models of the board state (Li et al., 2023a). In this work, we provide evidence of a closely related linear representation of the board. In particular, we show that probing for "my colour" vs. "opponent's colour" may be a simple yet powerful way to interpret the model's internal state. This precise understanding of the internal representations allows us to control the model's behaviour with simple vector arithmetic. Linear representations enable significant interpretability progress, which we demonstrate with further exploration of how the world model is computed.

papers.title: Data Distributional Properties Drive Emergent In-Context Learning in Transformers
papers.research_question: What aspects of the training regime lead to emergent in-context learning in transformers? Specifically, is it the transformer architecture or the distributional properties of the training data that are critical?
papers.core_contribution: In-context learning emerges in transformers when trained on data with specific distributional properties (burstiness, large numbers of rare classes, dynamic meanings), and a Zipfian distribution allows both in-context and in-weights learning to coexist. Architecture also matters, as recurrent models fail to show in-context learning under the same conditions.
papers.conclusion: Both data distributional properties and architecture are key to the emergence of in-context learning in transformers.
papers.key_findings:
Burstiness in training data promotes in-context learning but reduces in-weights learning.
A large number of rarely occurring training classes improves in-context learning.
Dynamic meanings (multiple labels per class or within-class variation) increase in-context learning.
Training on a Zipfian (skewed) distribution allows both in-context and in-weights learning to coexist in the same model.
Transformers exhibit in-context learning under these conditions, but recurrent models (RNN, LSTM) do not.
papers.limitation: The model implementation and evaluation procedure do not require the models to handle novel image labels, only novel image classes.
future_direction: How data distributional properties interact with reinforcement learning vs. supervised losses.
How results might differ in experiments that replicate other aspects of language and language modeling (e.g., symbolic inputs, next-token prediction, context-dependent word meaning).
Understanding the behaviors and biases of transformers vs. recurrent architectures.
papers.abstract: Large transformer-based models are able to perform in-context few-shot learning, without being explicitly trained for it. This observation raises the question: what aspects of the training regime lead to this emergent behavior? Here, we show that this behavior is driven by the distributions of the training data itself. In-context learning emerges when the training data exhibits particular distributional properties such as burstiness (items appear in clusters rather than being uniformly distributed over time) and having large numbers of rarely occurring classes. In-context learning also emerges more strongly when item meanings or interpretations are dynamic rather than fixed. These properties are exemplified by natural language, but are also inherent to naturalistic data in a wide range of other domains. They also depart significantly from the uniform, i.i.d. training distributions typically used for standard supervised learning. In our initial experiments, we found that in-context learning traded off against more conventional weight-based learning, and models were unable to achieve both simultaneously. However, our later experiments uncovered that the two modes of learning could co-exist in a single model when it was trained on data following a skewed Zipfian distribution -- another common property of naturalistic data, including language. In further experiments, we found that naturalistic data distributions were only able to elicit in-context learning in transformers, and not in recurrent models. In sum, our findings indicate how the transformer architecture works together with particular properties of the training data to drive the intriguing emergent in-context learning behaviour of large language models, and how future work might encourage both in-context and in-weights learning in domains beyond language.

papers.title: Large Language Models Know What Makes Exemplary Contexts
papers.research_question: How can LLMs self-select and optimize in-context examples to improve in-context learning performance?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a framework where LLMs self-select influential in-context examples via a parameter-efficient retrieval head trained with reinforcement learning based on the LLM's own preference, enhancing ICL performance.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents a unified framework that allows LLMs to actively select and rank influential examples and optimize demonstration selection via reinforcement learning, enhancing LLMs' ability to learn favorable contexts.
papers.key_findings:
RL-ICL outperforms random and dense retrieval baselines on most NLP tasks.
The reward model is necessary for effective reinforcement learning training.
The method selects more representative and diverse demonstrations for in-context learning.
ICL performance improves with the proposed sequential retrieval approach.
Performance gains saturate with more than three demonstrations, balancing computation and performance.
papers.limitation:
The corpus cannot accommodate new entries.
Computational costs escalate with an increasing number of demonstrations.
papers.abstract: In-context learning (ICL) has proven to be a significant capability with the advancement of Large Language models (LLMs). By instructing LLMs using few-shot demonstrative examples, ICL enables them to perform a wide range of tasks without needing to update millions of parameters. This paper presents a unified framework for LLMs that allows them to self-select influential in-context examples to compose their contexts; self-rank candidates with different demonstration compositions; self-optimize the demonstration selection and ordering through reinforcement learning. Specifically, our method designs a parameter-efficient retrieval head that generates the optimized demonstration after training with rewards from LLM's own preference. Experimental results validate the proposed method's effectiveness in enhancing ICL performance. Additionally, our approach effectively identifies and selects the most representative examples for the current task, and includes more diversity in retrieval.

papers.title: Language Steering for Multilingual In-Context Learning
papers.research_question: Does language identity occupy structured directions in activation space, and can a simple activation offset improve multilingual in-context learning?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces language vectors, a training-free method that improves multilingual in-context learning by steering activations, and shows that language identity occupies structured directions in activation space.
papers.conclusion: Language vectors improve multilingual in-context learning and encode meaningful linguistic structure, supporting the hypothesis that language identity occupies structured directions in activation space.
papers.key_findings:
Language vectors improve performance over baselines across tasks and languages.
Vectors encode linguistic structure, with related languages clustering together.
Vectors transfer across tasks, indicating they capture language-specific rather than task-specific information.
Steering is most effective in early to middle layers.
The method is training-free and requires no parameter updates.
papers.limitation:
Hyperparameters are selected per language via validation performance, which requires held-out data and may not generalize to new languages or domains.
Evaluation is limited to instruction-tuned decoder-only models.
Certain task transfers fail (e.g., MSVAMP to XNLI).
future_direction: Extending the approach to languages without parallel data.
Applying language vectors to generative tasks such as summarization.
Predicting steering effectiveness without exhaustive hyperparameter search.
papers.abstract: While multilingual large language models have gained widespread adoption, their performance on non-English languages remains substantially inferior to English. This disparity is particularly evident in in-context learning scenarios, where providing demonstrations in English but testing on non-English inputs leads to significant performance degradation. In this paper, we hypothesize that LLMs develop a universal semantic space for understanding languages, where different languages are encoded as distinct directions within this space. Based on this hypothesis, we propose language vectors -- a training-free language steering approach that leverages activation differences between source and target languages to guide model behavior. We steer the model generations by adding the vector to the intermediate model activations during inference. This is done to make the model's internal representations shift towards the target language space without any parameter updates. We evaluate our method across three datasets and test on a total of 19 languages on three different models. Our results show consistent improvements on multilingual in-context learning over baselines across all tasks and languages tested. Beyond performance gains, hierarchical clustering of steering vectors reveals meaningful linguistic structure aligned with language families. These vectors also successfully transfer across tasks, demonstrating that these representations are task-agnostic.

papers.title: The Same But Different: Structural Similarities and Differences in Multilingual Language Modeling
papers.research_question: When two languages employ the same morphosyntactic processes, do LLMs handle them using shared internal circuitry? When two languages require different morphosyntactic processes, do LLMs handle them using different internal circuitry?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that LLMs use shared internal circuitry for similar syntactic processes across languages, even in independently trained monolingual models, and employ language-specific components (e.g., feed-forward networks) for language-specific morphological processes.
papers.conclusion: The paper finds that cross-lingual structural similarity is represented within LLMs using shared circuits that invoke the same algorithm independent of language, and that language-specific processing is localized to play a causal role only in languages that require it.
papers.key_findings:
Multilingual models use a single circuit to handle the same syntactic process independently of the language in which it occurs.
Monolingual models trained independently on English and Chinese each adopt nearly the same circuit for the IOI task, suggesting consistency in how LLMs learn to handle this aspect of language modeling.
For tasks requiring language-specific morphological processes (e.g., past tense marking in English), multilingual models invoke a largely overlapping circuit but employ language-specific components as needed, such as feed-forward networks in English only for morphological marking.
The circuits identified for the IOI task align with prior work, indicating that the same mechanism is shared between English and Chinese within a multilingual model.
Heads specifically responsible for past tense disambiguation are activated in English but not in Chinese, and they suppress present-tense verbs in English.
papers.limitation: Results are limited to specific tasks and datasets, requiring future work for replication and generalization.
future_direction: Replicate and generalize findings to more tasks and datasets.
Explore cross-disciplinary collaborations to gain fresh perspectives on linguistic universality using LLMs.
Investigate whether circuit overlap can be exploited for improving cross-lingual transfer and safety.
papers.abstract: We employ new tools from mechanistic interpretability in order to ask whether the internal structure of large language models (LLMs) shows correspondence to the linguistic structures which underlie the languages on which they are trained. In particular, we ask (1) when two languages employ the same morphosyntactic processes, do LLMs handle them using shared internal circuitry? and (2) when two languages require different morphosyntactic processes, do LLMs handle them using different internal circuitry? Using English and Chinese multilingual and monolingual models, we analyze the internal circuitry involved in two tasks. We find evidence that models employ the same circuit to handle the same syntactic process independently of the language in which it occurs, and that this is the case even for monolingual models trained completely independently. Moreover, we show that multilingual models employ language-specific components (attention heads and feed-forward networks) when needed to handle linguistic processes (e.g., morphological marking) that only exist in some languages. Together, our results provide new insights into how LLMs trade off between exploiting common structures and preserving linguistic differences when tasked with modeling multiple languages simultaneously.

papers.title: An Analysis of Encoder Representations in Transformer-Based Machine Translation
papers.research_question: What kind of linguistic information (syntactic and semantic) is learned by the encoder of Transformer-based machine translation models, and how does it vary across layers and models with different translation quality?
papers.core_contribution: The paper analyzes encoder representations in Transformer-based machine translation and finds that specific attention heads capture syntactic dependencies, with lower layers encoding more syntax and higher layers more semantics.
papers.conclusion: The experimental evaluation sheds light on interesting findings about dependency relations and syntactic and semantic behavior across layers in Transformer encoder representations.
papers.key_findings:
Each layer has at least one attention head that encodes a significant amount of syntactic dependencies.
Lower layers tend to encode more syntactic information, while upper layers move towards semantic tasks.
The information about the length of the input sentence starts to vanish after the third layer.
Attention can be used to transfer knowledge between high- and low-resource languages, improving translation quality.
future_direction: Extend the analysis with probing tasks to evaluate other linguistic properties.
Use a recent evaluation dataset for analysis.
Analyze the attention weights between the encoder and the decoder.
papers.abstract: The attention mechanism is a successful technique in modern NLP, especially in tasks like machine translation. The recently proposed network architecture of the Transformer is based entirely on attention mechanisms and achieves new state of the art results in neural machine translation, outperforming other sequence-to-sequence models. However, so far not much is known about the internal properties of the model and the representations it learns to achieve that performance. To study this question, we investigate the information that is learned by the attention mechanism in Transformer models with different translation quality. We assess the representations of the encoder by extracting dependency relations based on self-attention weights, we perform four probing tasks to study the amount of syntactic and semantic captured information and we also test attention in a transfer learning scenario. Our analysis sheds light on the relative strengths and weaknesses of the various encoder representations. We observe that specific attention heads mark syntactic dependency relations and we can also confirm that lower layers tend to learn more about syntax while higher layers tend to encode more semantics.

papers.title: Evaluating Transformer's Ability to Learn Mildly Context-Sensitive Languages
papers.research_question: How well do Transformers learn mildly context-sensitive languages (MCSLs) from finite examples, in terms of generalizing to in-distribution data and extrapolating to longer strings? What kind of meaningful representations or patterns do the models learn?
papers.core_contribution: This paper empirically evaluates the Transformer's ability to learn a variety of mildly context-sensitive languages (MCSLs), finding that while they generalize well to in-distribution data, their ability to extrapolate to longer strings is worse than that of LSTMs. Analyses show the learned self-attention patterns model dependency relations and representations encode count information.
papers.conclusion: Transformers can learn mildly context-sensitive languages from finite examples and leverage self-attention to model dependency relations, but their extrapolation ability is limited compared to LSTMs. The learned patterns and behaviors provide insights into the models' linguistic capacity.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers generalize well to unseen in-distribution data for MCSLs, performing comparably to LSTMs.
Transformers' ability to extrapolate to longer strings (out-of-distribution) is limited and generally worse than LSTMs.
Removing sinusoidal positional encoding in Transformer decoders (next character prediction tasks) can improve extrapolation ability.
Learned self-attention patterns often reflect the symbol dependency relations within the string (e.g., checkerboard patterns for crossing dependencies).
For the complex scramble language MIX, the learned representations encode count information for symbol occurrences, which may aid in solving the language.
papers.limitation:
The empirical study is bounded by a string length upper bound, so the dataset is bounded and might form a language with reduced complexity, weakening arguments about general learnability.
The roles of other heads, the feed-forward sublayer, etc. are not investigated, so it cannot be definitively said how self-attention directly contributed to inference.
papers.abstract: Despite the fact that Transformers perform well in NLP tasks, recent studies suggest that self-attention is theoretically limited in learning even some regular and context-free languages. These findings motivated us to think about their implications in modeling natural language, which is hypothesized to be mildly context-sensitive. We test the Transformer's ability to learn mildly context-sensitive languages of varying complexities, and find that they generalize well to unseen in-distribution data, but their ability to extrapolate to longer strings is worse than that of LSTMs. Our analyses show that the learned self-attention patterns and representations modeled dependency relations and demonstrated counting behavior, which may have helped the models solve the languages.

papers.title: When Parts Are Greater Than Sums: Individual LLM Components Can Outperform Full Models
papers.research_question: How do individual components (attention heads and MLPs) behave in in-context learning, and can they outperform the full model?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that individual attention heads and MLPs can have higher accuracy than the full model in ICL, and proposes component reweighting, a method to learn to scale component contributions from few-shot examples, improving ICL accuracy.
papers.conclusion: The decomposition provides a new perspective on ICL, revealing consistent component characteristics, and motivates a practical method (component reweighting) that improves ICL accuracy.
papers.key_findings:
Good-performing components exist that individually outperform the full model on classification tasks.
Bad-performing components perform below chance accuracy.
Label-biased components always predict the same label regardless of input.
Component accuracies are consistent across different demonstration sets and contrastive templates.
Component reweighting, which learns to scale component contributions from few labeled examples, improves ICL accuracy over standard ICL.
papers.limitation:
Component reweighting requires a small set of labeled data for training the weights.
The method is only experimented with classification tasks, leaving generation tasks for future work.
The paper does not focus on circuits, so mechanistic understanding of components is limited.
future_direction: Generalize the method to generation tasks.
papers.abstract: This paper studies in-context learning by decomposing the output of large language models into the individual contributions of attention heads and MLPs (components). We observe curious components: good-performing ones that individually do well on a classification task, even when the model performs poorly; bad-performing ones that do much worse than chance; and label-biased components that always predict the same label. We find that component accuracies are well-correlated across different demonstration sets and perturbations of prompt templates. Based on our findings, we propose component reweighting, which learns to linearly re-scale the component activations from a few labeled examples. Given 24 labeled examples, our method improves by an average of 6.0% accuracy points over 24-shot ICL across 8 tasks on Llama-2-7B. Overall, this paper both enriches our understanding of ICL and provides a practical method for improvement by examining model internals.

papers.title: Structural Supervision Improves Few-Shot Learning and Syntactic\n Generalization in Neural Language Models
papers.research_question: How well do neural language models learn syntactic properties from few examples, and can they generalize these properties across syntactic transformations?
papers.core_contribution: Neural language models can learn syntactic generalizations from minimal exposure and show syntactic invariance, with structural supervision improving accuracy and invariance.
papers.conclusion: Neural language models are capable of few-shot syntactic learning and show some syntactic invariance, with structural supervision enhancing these abilities.
papers.key_findings:
Neural models induce proper syntactic generalizations for nominal number and verbal argument structure after just two or three exposures during training.
